Leveraging the broad wavelength coverage of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), we present new near- and mid-infrared observations tracing the ionization stratification of these outflows with a unified dataset. We analyze emission lines originating from molecular gas to highly ionized plasma and analyze the ionized gas using a 5-component Cloudy photoionization model covering three primary phases. Applying the footprint line method to characterize the X-ray emitting gas, we find that it holds the largest share of the total mass, suggesting that it is a primary candidate for driving AGN feedback in this system.

title: Positivity of simplicial volume of convex projective manifolds
abstract: Let $Ω$ be an irreducible properly convex projective domain admitting a discrete cocompact group action of projective automorphisms. We prove that the Holmes--Thompson volumes of projective simplices with vertices in $Ω$ are uniformly bounded. As a consequence, we prove that a closed properly convex projective manifold of dimension at least two has positive simplicial volume if and only if it is irreducible.

title: Torsion phenomena in symplectic capacities via Clarke duality
abstract: We study Gutt--Hutchings capacities with finite cyclic coefficients and show that torsion in positive $S^1$-equivariant symplectic homology detects new obstructions to symplectic embeddings between convex toric domains. Prime-field coefficients give no additional obstructions in this class, while the torsion responsible for the new obstructions already appears over $\mathbb Z/p^{p+2}$ for every prime $p$. We prove a stabilization theorem for these capacities on convex bodies with arbitrary commutative coefficients, yielding a sharp stabilized embedding obstruction in an explicit example. Clarke duality makes these phenomena accessible to computation. We extend the filtered equivariant Clarke--Floer comparison to arbitrary commutative coefficient rings and compute the capacities using models of dual action sublevels built from representation spheres. The circle-action weights encode orbit covering multiplicities, whose products govern the new obstructions.

title: A Polynomial Time Approximation for the Minimization of Implication Systems and Horn CNFs
abstract: An implication system is a collection of rules of the form $B \imp H$, where the set $B$ of Boolean variables is the {\em body} of the rule, while $H$ is the set of its {\em heads}. Such a rule is an aggregate representation of individual implications $B\imp h$, for $h\in H$ which correspond to the clauses of an equivalent CNF representation of a Horn Boolean function. An implication system is {\em body-minimum}/{\em clause-minimum} if it has the minimum number of bodies/clauses among all logically equivalent implication systems. The corresponding minimization problems appear not only in the context of implication systems, but also as problems for closure systems, directed hypergraphs, representation of dependencies in relational databases, or in Horn CNF minimization. While body-minimization is known to be solvable in polynomial time (and there are several algorithms in the literature that solve this task), clause-minimization is known to be NP-hard. In fact, body-minimization has a particular canonical solution, called the GD-basis of the underlying Horn function that also can be computed efficiently. In this paper, we utilize a known connection between the two minimization problems stating that for every implication system there always exists a logically equivalent clause-minimum implication system which has the same bodies as its canonical GD-basis, see (B{é}rczi and B{é}rczi-Kov{á}cs, 2017), and (Adaricheva and Nation, 2014). We use this fact to design a polynomial time approximation algorithm which for any $δ>0$ outputs a $(\frac{1}{4} + δ)n$-factor approximation of the logically equivalent clause-minimum implication system on $n$ variables. This is an improvement from the best known algorithm so far that provides only an $(n-1)$-factor approximation, see (Hammer and Kogan, 1993).

title: A Proof of Stein's Equidissection Conjecture
abstract: In 1970 Monsky showed that a square cannot be dissected into an odd number of equal-area triangles. His proof used an ingenious colouring of the plane based on a 2-adic valuation on $\mathbb{R}$ together with Sperner's lemma. Subsequent work established similar results for regular polygons, centrally symmetric polygons, and polyominoes. In 2000, Stein proposed a common generalisation of the centrally symmetric and polyomino cases to balanced polygons. In 2014, Rudenko introduced a new perspective on the problem and proved Stein's conjecture for dissections with rational vertex coordinates. Building on and streamlining his approach, we resolve the conjecture in full.

title: EvoMem3D: Adaptive-Depth Temporal Representation Memory for Multi-Camera 3D Detection
abstract: Modern multi-camera 3D detectors increasingly rely on large Vision Transformer (ViT) image encoders, making repeated full-depth encoding a dominant inference cost even though adjacent driving frames are highly redundant. We present EvoMem3D, an adaptive-depth temporal framework that caches the most recent full-depth detector-interface appearance representation as a read-only anchor and combines it with policy-selected partial features from the current frame. A lightweight pre-encoding controller chooses among semantic encoder exits before image processing, allocating shallow computation to stable frames and deeper computation when the visual state changes. To reuse appearance without carrying stale geometry, we decouple temporal appearance from geometric alignment: current-frame calibration defines the decoder geometry at every timestamp, while a motion-conditioned positional adapter accounts for anchor-to-current ego motion. On nuScenes, EvoMem3D achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP while reducing end-to-end latency from 364.4 to 168.7 ms (x2.16) relative to standard dense DETR3D. With StreamPETR, it reaches 61.36 NDS and 52.55 mAP at a x1.92 speedup. Controlled studies isolate the effects of current evidence, temporal reuse, memory correction, and adaptive routing, while our audit confirms that the policy learns to distinguish semantic driving regimes.

title: Markets for Compute and Inference: Structure, Financing, and Risk Transfer
abstract: Capacity to run large language models is rented by the accelerator-hour, and their output is sold by the million tokens. Both goods now have published price indices, an over-the-counter forward has traded on one, a perpetual future on one is listed offshore, and CME and ICE have specified futures on rental indices that await the United States regulator. We ask what in these two markets can be hedged, by whom, and at what price. Three findings stand out. First, the price that exchange contracts settle on is not the price that drives operators' revenue. Every contract references the published short-dated rental rate, while most revenue, and with it credit quality, comes from private multi-year contracts whose prices are largely undisclosed. Second, the token price and the rental rate are linked by an identity through throughput and margin, but they are different exposures, so a hedge on the rental rate does not hedge the cost of inference; at the measured capability of GPT-5 the cheapest list price fell by a factor of 17 in twelve months, and by far less at lower capability. Third, the demand for hedging already sits in credit agreements, as the years by which operators' debt outlives their contracted revenue. Filings cannot measure that gap, because debt is scheduled year by year while contracted revenue rarely is, and the one loan that prices it settles the risk by cash prepayment against a model only the parties see. We design a reverse convertible note through which leveraged operators could buy protection against falling rental rates. Its coupon depends steeply on the annualised volatility of the rental rate, which the two public indices put between about 5% and 89% according to how each is built and the horizon measured; across that range the fair one-year coupon runs from 4.1% to 31.5%.

title: Achievable Information Rate for FTN under a Reduced Complexity BCJR Receiver
abstract: The capacity of faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) signaling in additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels has been established and is achieved by Gaussian inputs. However, the capacity of FTN signaling with finite-constellations is not yet fully characterized. The achievable information rate (AIR) provides a lower bound on this constrained capacity by quantifying the rate supported by a specified input distribution and receiver. This paper investigates the AIR of FTN signaling with finite constellations using full-state and reduced-state Bahl-Cocke-Jelinek-Raviv (BCJR) receivers, with bidirectional decision feedback incorporated into the reduced-state receiver. Especially, the detection problem is formulated in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), where a geometric foundation is established to understand FTN under severe time packing. The formulation establishes that the Ungerboeck metric remains valid even when the noise covariance is singular. We further characterize detection errors geometrically using RKHS distances between competing sequences. We also study outage probability for reduced-state detection, which occurs when AIR is zero, in addition to deriving the zero-AIR outage criterion for reduced-state detection. Unlike ISI-free Nyquist signaling, reduced-state FTN detection can retain residual ISI that causes the receiver to assign excessive confidence to incorrect symbols, leading to outage even at high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Our results confirm both the spectral efficiency gains and the feasibility of FTN systems employing finite constellations and realistic receiver architectures.

title: Right Goal, Wrong Body: Re-grounding Frozen VLAs under Actuation Shift
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are capable of producing desired robotic behaviors in ideal settings. However, they often fail when the robot's actuation changes at deployment. For example, remounting, mechanical wear, or command latency changes can lead to failed tasks and unsafe behaviors. To address the inevitable actuation shift, we propose ReGround, an inference-time method that keeps the VLA frozen and re-grounds its intended motion. ReGround learns the deployed robot's dynamics from task-agnostic motor babbling, and then tracks the policy's intended motion while staying close to the policy's own plan. ReGround activates only upon detecting a shift, and needs no rewards, demonstrations, or retraining. We show via two VLAs, eight LIBERO tasks, and five shift settings that ReGround can restore near-oracle success, such as raising $π_{0.5}$'s success from 0.16 to 0.90 under 400 ms latency, while remaining safer than a linear-calibration baseline. Project website and open-source code: https://umersiddique94.github.io/ReGround/.

title: From XR Sketches to CAD: Preserving Design Intent with AI
abstract: Extended reality (XR) allows designers to sketch shapes directly in 3D, but converting these sketches into editable, feature-based CAD requires interpreting their intent. A sketch may contain drawing errors, intended features, and design choices that remain open. Correcting every irregularity risks erasing intended features, while automatic completion may impose choices the designer has not made. We argue that AI should add precision without overriding design intent, considering both the resulting shape and how the CAD model behaves during later edits. To guide this process, we propose a conceptual framework that distinguishes errors from intentions in individual sketch properties and relates them to correction, preservation, and exploration in editable CAD. We also outline five research directions for sketch interpretation, CAD construction, and evaluation, with testable hypotheses for selected questions.

title: TileCache: Serving Multi-Round Diffusion Image Editing with Compressed Activation Caches
abstract: Multi-round diffusion image editing can reduce computation by reusing intermediate activations, but retaining these activations across editing rounds introduces substantial memory and bandwidth overheads. Compression can reduce these overheads, but efficient cache construction is challenging: compressing only after editing requires buffering over 100 GB of activations per request. Moreover, the compressed cache must support selective reuse, as future masked edits require only a subset of the cached activations. It also exposes a scheduling challenge, as cached edits are faster than initial generations, causing naive policies to severely delay either initial generations or editing requests. In this paper, we aim to address both challenges through compression-informed serving. We develop TileCache, a serving system for multi-round diffusion editing. It compresses reusable activations and incorporates a scheduler that balances both edits and initial generation requests. Compared with the state-of-the-art image editing baseline, TileCache sustains over 2x the request arrival rate at 90% SLO attainment. It completes edits 2.4-4.5x and initial generations 1.3-2.2x faster than the baseline, while preserving image quality.

title: Machine Learning the $GW$ Self-Energy Operator for Real Materials
abstract: Machine learning of $GW$ in solids has largely focused on prediction of scalar quasiparticle energy corrections. Here, we introduce a phase-aware many-body transformer that predicts the full $\mathbf{k}$-resolved complex self-energy matrix. As a proof of principle, we apply the model to predict quasiparticle energies before and after diagonalization of the quasiparticle Hamiltonian, obtaining a test set mean absolute error (MAE) of 29 meV for a dataset of 1745 2D materials in the static COHSEX approximation and 60 meV for a more limited dataset of 433 materials calculated within a plasmon-pole model. COHSEX pretraining followed by finetuning reduces this MAE to 42 meV. The predicted matrices also accurately reproduce QP wavefunctions.

title: Logarithmic thermodynamic cost of prediction from rare observations
abstract: A memory predicting changes in its environment from rare observations must spend energy on sampling and recording. We consider autonomous chemical memories driven by a sample-and-hold sensor observing an environment that switches at rate gamma, with sampling frequency f<<gamma. An ideal observer with access to the full observation history can retain predictive information proportional to f. However, retaining a finite fraction of this information in an autonomous physical memory requires work of order kBT ln(gamma/f) per sensor change. This additional thermodynamic cost arises from the competing requirements of suppressing false records during long intervals between observations and responding rapidly to new observations. We establish a universal low-power bound on predictive information, which grows at most as P/ln(P_ref/P) with power budget P, uniformly over any finite number of memory states and independently of network topology and memory relaxation times. We further demonstrate that memory architecture determines the attainable scaling. With bounded transition rates and readout from the memory alone, two-state memories are limited to P^2 scaling, whereas a three-state memory is sufficient to attain the optimal logarithmic scaling. Our results establish a fundamental thermodynamic distinction between acquiring information and maintaining a useful record of a changing environment.

title: Uniform compactness in a family of $\bar{\partial}$-Neumann problems
abstract: In their paper on non-coercive boundary value problems, Kohn and Nirenberg show that a priori estimates for all forms satisfying $\bar{\partial}$-Neumann boundary conditions follow from a compactness estimate. Inspired by Hamilton, we show that these a priori estimates are stable under deformations of the complex structure, the hermitian metric and the volume form of the underlying manifold. We use a parameter $m$ to encode a deformation of this data. We show that if a family of $\bar{\partial}$-Neumann problems depends smoothly on $m$ and the compactness estimate(s) hold (with constants uniform in $m$), then the family of solution operators also depends smoothly $m$. As a consequence we obtain sufficient conditions for the Bergman kernel to vary smoothly in a family of domains. We also provide a sufficient condition for the uniform compactness estimate(s) to hold in a family of domains.

title: Asymptotic radial symmetry of $p$-Ginzburg-Landau minimizers on the disk
abstract: We solve the minimizer case of Brezis's Open Problem~2.3 for every fixed $p>2$. For $\varepsilon>0$, let $\mathbf{u}_{\varepsilon}\in W^{1,p}(B_1;\mathbb{R}^2)$ be a global minimizer of the $p$-Ginzburg--Landau energy \[ \int_{B_1} \left( \frac{|\nabla\mathbf{u}|^p}{p} +\frac{(1-|\mathbf{u}|^2)^2}{4\varepsilon^2} \right)\,dx \] with prescribed trace $\mathbf{u}_{\varepsilon}|_{\partial B_1}(x)=x$. We prove that, as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, $\mathbf{u}_{\varepsilon}(x)\to x/|x|$ at every point $x\in B_1\setminus\{0\}$. The convergence is strong in $W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_1\setminus\{0\};\mathbb{R}^2)$ and hence uniform on every compact subset of the punctured disk. On each such compact subset, the potential energy tends to zero and the total energy converges to the $p$-Dirichlet energy of the radial map. No symmetry or uniqueness of the minimizers is assumed. The proof combines whole-plane concentration, a strict exterior filling estimate, and quantitative convexity to locate the concentration point and identify the limiting map.

title: Improving Tropical Cyclone Forecasts through Objective Ensemble Track-Error Reduction
abstract: Accurate tropical cyclone (TC) track guidance is essential for warnings, evacuation planning, and risk communication, but outlying members and distinct track scenarios can degrade raw ensemble forecasts. Statistical and machine-learning (ML) methods proposed to improve ensemble guidance are difficult to compare because previous studies often use different forecast systems, basins, periods, and verification methods. Using a common verification framework, this study compares six objective methods (four statistical trimming and two ML methods) with the full ensemble mean for 138 TCs forecast by GEFS, MOGREPS-G, and IFS during 2016-2024. Dynamic trimming (DT) is the most consistent statistical method, reducing mean total track error by 8.0%, 13.4%, and 16.1% at short, medium, and long ranges. Its largest benefits occur in high-spread cases, where it can reach 70% of the low-error bound. Short-lead-error trimming (SLET) provides useful delayed guidance after early observations become available, but its improvement decreases with lead time. Regression-mixture clustering (RC) shows potential in low-spread cases and provides the largest improvement over the control run. The gradient boosted tree (GBT) produces the largest medium-range improvement and exceeds the theoretical trimming bound, suggesting strong potential, particularly when the observed track is poorly represented by the ensemble family. However, its 12.8% short-range degradation and gains concentrated in a small subset of cases indicate overcorrection when the ensemble mean is already accurate, highlighting the need for additional constraints. These results provide a consistent basis for using objective error-reduction methods to strengthen TC track guidance for operational decision-making.

title: Contraction Analysis and Control of Polynomial Dynamical Systems
abstract: Contraction analysis has found broad applications in synchronization, tracking, observer design, and nonlinear feedback control. However, establishing contraction conditions for polynomial dynamical systems remains challenging due to their state-dependent Jacobians. In this article, we develop a tensor-based framework for contraction analysis of polynomial dynamical systems by exploiting the structure of orthogonally decomposable (odeco) coefficient tensors. By transforming the dynamics into modal coordinates, we derive necessary and sufficient semicontraction conditions and characterize state-dependent semimetrics. We establish fundamental limitations on exponential contraction and prove polynomial decay of differential displacements on forward-invariant regions. To accommodate more general polynomial dynamical systems, we extend the framework to include linear dynamics and non-odeco tensor perturbations, deriving computationally tractable contraction certificates with explicit robustness guarantees. We further develop convex feedback synthesis conditions based on linear matrix inequalities for general input matrices. We demonstrate the effectiveness and computational scalability of the proposed framework through numerical experiments on both synthetic systems and nonlinear elastic relaxation models.

title: Integrating Latent Block Models into Variational Autoencoders for Disentangled Representation Learning
abstract: We introduce LBM-VAE, a novel framework that integrates Latent Block Models (LBMs) into Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to jointly cluster observations and latent dimensions. Beyond its clustering capabilities, LBM-VAE provides a block-structured latent representation that naturally supports disentangled representation learning. In contrast to conventional approaches that associate each factor of variation with an individual latent dimension, our framework allows factors of variation to be encoded across groups of latent dimensions. Experimental results demonstrate the promising clustering performance of LBM-VAE, while achieving competitive results in disentangled representation learning. LBM-VAE highlights the potential of combining co-clustering and variational inference to learn structured and interpretable latent representations.

title: VoxMel TTS Technical Report
abstract: Continuous autoregressive TTS relies on an acoustic target that enables stable next-latent modeling while preserving fine-grained acoustic details. While existing approaches employ learned compressed representations (e.g., continuous VAE latents) to render prediction tractable, they rely on complex neural encoders that often cap generation fidelity. Conversely, training-free targets like mel-spectrograms eliminate encoder overhead, yet their potential for autoregressive generation remains largely underexplored. In this work, we propose VoxMel, a tokenizer-free framework for autoregressive TTS that makes stable mel modeling tractable through a fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar transform. The transform first decomposes each mel spectrogram along frequency into local averages and a frequency residual, then splits the averaged component along time into Coarse-Mel and a temporal residual. A language-model backbone with a flow-matching head autoregressively generates Coarse-Mel. Non-autoregressive residual tiers then predict the temporal residual from Coarse-Mel, followed by the frequency residual conditioned on the reconstructed Frequency-Averaged Mel. Neither residual is fed back into the autoregressive history. Trained on 100K hours of Emilia, the supervised 0.6B model obtains 1.51\% WER and 0.738 speaker similarity (SIM) on test-en, and 1.29\% CER and 0.755 SIM on test-zh. GRPO improves these results to 1.15\% WER / 0.753 SIM and 1.17\% CER / 0.776 SIM, respectively. We also distill the guided flow head into two- and four-step students, requiring 2 or 4 head evaluations per coarse frame. The four-step student retains competitive SIM and nearly matches the supervised model in WER/CER.

title: Deep Sequence Model for Genome Wide Discovery of Coding and Regulatory Element Signatures
abstract: Interpreting deep neural networks for genomic sequence classification remains challenging despite strong predictive performance. We develop a lightweight CNN with post-training gradient-based analysis to identify which sequence positions drive coding versus intergenomic classification. Applied to the standardized demo_coding_vs_intergenomic_seqs dataset, our model achieves 91.87% validation accuracy while revealing interpretable patterns: nine hot spots with consistently high importance, clear class-specific separation at positions 20-100 (coding) and 150-190 (intergenomic), and a strong mean-variance correlation (r = 0.530) indicating robust discriminative features. Gradient-based importance analysis shows that the model implicitly learns biologically meaningful sequence distinctions without explicit annotations. This work demonstrates that neural network interpretability and accuracy can coexist, providing a framework for understanding genomic sequence classification and enabling biology-driven hypothesis generation.

title: Continuous-Time Stochastic Contraction Induced by Common White Noise
abstract: This paper studies contraction properties of stochastic dynamical systems governed by Itô stochastic differential equations. We consider two trajectories driven by a common noise process and measure their separation using Finsler distances, which encompass Riemannian and norm-induced distances. Two notions of contraction are then investigated: $L^p$-contraction, defined by exponential decay of the $L^p$-norm (or the $p$-th moment) of the distance, and almost sure contraction, defined by exponential decay of the distance along almost every sample path. Each notion is characterized by a differential condition that is necessary and sufficient for contraction under mild hypotheses. Relations between contraction notions and an associated incremental input-to-state stability result are also established. As an illustration, we apply the established theory to analyze noise-induced synchronization and quantify its robustness with respect to parameter perturbations.

title: Tight Bounds for Non-Monotone Submodular Maximization under a Cardinality Constraint with Constant Recourse
abstract: We study the maximization of a nonnegative submodular function under a cardinality constraint when elements arrive one at a time and an algorithm must report a feasible set after every arrival. The recourse of an algorithm is the largest number of insertions and deletions that it makes to the reported set at a single arrival. For every $ε>0$, we give an algorithm with recourse $O(ε^{-2})$ whose reported set has, at every time, expected value at least $1/4-ε$ times the largest value of a feasible set of arrived elements. The algorithm evaluates the function polynomially often, and only on sets of arrived elements. We also show that no algorithm with constant recourse achieves a ratio above $1/4$, even if it knows the function and the arrival order in advance and has unlimited computation, and that any fixed ratio above $1/4$ requires recourse that grows as a positive power of the cardinality budget. Thus $1/4$ is the optimal limiting ratio with constant recourse. The previous best ratio with constant recourse was $3-2\sqrt2\approx0.172$. Our algorithm assigns selection probabilities of at most one half and maintains, as elements arrive, an inequality bounding the value of every feasible set by a multiple of the expected value of a random set drawn with these probabilities; the reported set moves to a rounding of these probabilities through gradual replacements. The upper bound uses a weighted directed graph whose vertices arrive in groups of decreasing sizes.

title: Microfitting: Continual Learning via Cached Test-Time Training
abstract: Continual learning is a promising approach to specialize language models to an organization's private data. However, current methods exhibit a number of drawbacks including catastrophic forgetting, where new training updates overwrite prior knowledge. We present microfitting, which trains and caches a small adapter for each document. Each adapter is trained once, offline, on synthetic questions targeted at demonstrated base-model shortcomings and reused whenever that document is queried. This method borrows from test-time learning literature and sidesteps the problem of continual learning through parameter isolation, allowing the system to specialize on new data without overwriting prior knowledge. The process that generates adapter training data also improves over time, revising its recipe from previous outcomes and fresh examples of the target workload. On DeepSeek V4 Flash, microfitting substantially improves accuracy over the base model. In Enterprise Document Operations (EDO), an open-book Q&A environment over real-world enterprise documents, our method achieves a 38.2% relative improvement over base-model performance. Microfitting makes continual specialization practical and cost-efficient: a frozen model can adapt to an evolving private corpus overnight on local hardware, without modifying the base model or previously cached adapters.

title: Scaling large language model-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication with human-in-the-loop evidence-calibrated selection
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the ability to scale clinical adjudication tasks traditionally dependent on exhaustive manual review. Line-of-therapy (LoT) adjudication, a major bottleneck in oncology cohort construction, is a prime example. Line boundaries must be inferred from longitudinal treatment histories according to nuanced, study-specific definitions, at every regimen transition for every patient. LLMs can apply this adjudication at scale, but their reliability varies across patients. Treatment histories differ in complexity, and ambiguous or atypical patterns depend on expert clinical judgment. Reliable automation thus requires verified support for model assignments and the ability to identify cases that warrant manual review. Here, we present evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework for scaling LLM-assisted LoT adjudication. ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and returns completed adjudications to the model as precedent. As the evidence base grows, ECS continuously calibrates confidence to estimate residual error, thus enabling more efficient use of clinician time. In simulations on 136 clinician adjudicated patients with multiple myeloma, ECS achieved a residual error of 5% after review of 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% when review was directed by LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling. These results support a scalable approach to study-specific LoT adjudication, using clinician evidence to inform automated predictions, minimize error, and reduce review burden.

title: Oxygens breathe, electrons jump
abstract: Electronic transport in polyanionic battery cathodes proceeds through small-polaron hopping between transition-metal sites and is commonly assumed to be tightly coupled to the motion of charge-compensating mobile ions. Using olivine Li$_x$MnPO$_4$ as a prototypical platform, we use first-principles molecular dynamics with extended Hubbard functionals to follow, in real time and at finite temperature, the adiabatic evolution of Mn oxidation states and atomic sublattices. We find that polaron hopping and cation migration are dynamically decoupled: Mn$^{2+}$/Mn$^{3+}$ valence exchanges occur frequently while the intercalated ions remain confined to their sites, and hopping is gated by the local oxygen framework. Freezing the six oxygen atoms of an individual MnO$_6$ octahedron excludes that site from the hopping network, while increasing the fictitious oxygen mass slows down electronic transport. Each valence exchange coincides with a concerted breathing of the donor and acceptor octahedra ($ΔV \simeq 2$ $Å^3$), with their volume asymmetry crossing zero at the transition, consistent with the Holstein-Marcus coincidence condition. The hopping rate yields an activation energy of $E_a = 0.20 \pm 0.03$ eV, closely matching the elastic energy scale of the two coordination cages ($λ_V/4 \approx 0.20$ eV). These results identify the oxygen coordination cage, not the mobile cation sublattice, as the dynamical gate for small-polaron transport: a site can accept the electron only if its cage can breathe, and the barrier is governed by cage elasticity. Selective constraints and mass scaling applied to first-principles dynamics provide a general route to link electronic and lattice degrees of freedom in redox-active materials, opening the door to framework engineering in intercalation and mixed ionic-electronic conductors.

title: Estimating Outpatient Visit Prices from Hospital Price Transparency Data using Large Language Models
abstract: Objective: Hospital care prices in the United States have increased substantially, yet patients lack effective tools to access and compare costs. We aimed to develop and evaluate an LLM-based approach for improving access to and use of hospital price transparency (PT) data. Materials and Methods: To estimate visit prices, we used a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework to analyze PT files from three major hospitals in Maryland and the surrounding region. We compared BM25, OpenAI embedding models, and a GPT-BM25 hybrid against a no-RAG baseline for cost estimation of individual procedures and procedure groups, then evaluated the best approach for symptom-based visit cost estimation using synthetic simulations. Results: Across hospitals, the GPT-BM25 retriever achieved the best performance, with average price MAPE of 19.44% for individual procedures and 4.90% for groups, compared with 147.98% and 82.82%, respectively, for the no-RAG baseline. In simulations, our framework correctly identified approximately 50% of reference procedures and reduced MAPE relative to the LLM-only baseline at two of the three hospitals, while achieving comparable performance at the third. Discussion: Our framework uses RAG to improve care price estimation in real-world settings. Compared with the no-RAG baseline, it substantially improved cost estimates for both individual procedures and procedure groups. Improvements were smaller in synthetic simulations, likely because inferring procedures from clinical information is more complex. Practical challenges remain, including heterogeneous PT file formats, unexplained duplicate entries, and limited availability of insurer-negotiated rates. Conclusion: LLMs that effectively integrate PT data show strong potential to provide patients with more accessible and accurate healthcare cost estimates.

title: A counterexample to the subgraphings approximate the cost problem
abstract: We prove that for every $k\ge 2$, the free group $\mathbb{F}_k$ on $k$ generators admits a finite generating set $S$ such that the Schreier graphing of the Bernoulli action of $\mathbb{F}_k$ with respect to $S$ does not admit spanning subgraphings that would approximate the cost of the action. In particular, this gives an example of a graphing that spans a treeable countable pmp equivalence relation, but does not admit a spanning subtreeing.

title: Self-doped correlated adatom lattices on cubic boron nitride
abstract: We survey triangular adatom lattices on the (111) surfaces of cubic boron nitride (cBN) for strongly correlated two-dimensional electron systems. Using density functional theory combined with the constrained random phase approximation and charge self-consistent dynamical mean-field theory, we identify twelve promising candidates. Group-III (group-V) adatoms on the N- (B-)termination realize clean one-band Hubbard systems, while group-III and transition-metal (V, Cr, Mn) adatoms on the B-termination realize two-band Hubbard systems. Importantly, the polar III-V character of cBN induces self-doping by $\pm 1/4$ electron away from integer filling. With strong Hubbard (and Hund's) interactions and small hoppings, most systems are doped Mott insulators. Heavy quasielectrons with mass renormalizations up to 4 and strong local moments up to 2.5 $μ_B$ put our systems into a regime where unconventional superconductivity on the triangular lattice has been predicted.

title: Global dynamics of large smooth solutions to the two-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes system with Navier-slip boundary conditions
abstract: We establish global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions containing vacuum to the two-dimensional barotropic compressible Navier-Stokes equations with bulk viscosity depending on the density, in smooth bounded simply connected domains, subject to the Navier-slip boundary conditions. Without any restriction on the size of initial data, we obtain time-uniform density and velocity bounds and exponentialconvergence to equilibrium in Sobolev spaces for the density and velocity. Moreover an initial vacuum point will persist and force the exponential growth of density gradients.

title: Geometry-Derived Capacitance Dyadics with Floquet Sideband Correction for Anisotropic Periodic Patch Metasurfaces
abstract: Homogenised sheet models describe periodic metallic patch layers using a scalar sheet capacitance, which is only valid when the effective response is isotropic. An isotropic response exists for unit cells with patch geometries that have rotational symmetry of order three or higher. Lower-symmetry unit cells with irregular or random geometries generically require a full 2 x 2 surface-capacitance dyadic. We present a framework that computes this dyadic directly from the arbitrary gap-connected patch geometry on a unit cell of a hexagonal lattice. The two-dimensional Bravais periodicity fixes the two independent macroscopic loading directions, the connectivity of the gap ensures a full-rank response for the geometries considered here, and the point-group symmetry of the patch constrains the form of the dyadic. A quasi-static boundary value problem on a single periodic cell then determines its independent entries. We use the surface-capacitance dyadic in the anisotropic surface- wave dispersion relation, which includes the leading spatially-dispersive first shell Floquet-sideband correction. For each new patch geometry, the dyadic and the first-shell correction are obtained from a single quasi-static cell problem and from the reconstructed boundary. So anisotropic surface- wave dispersion follows without a per-geometry full-wave eigenmode band sweep or sheet-tensor retrieval. We validate this geometry-to-dispersion chain against full-wave eigenmode simulations across six representative symmetry classes, showing that the correction captures band flattening near the Brillouin-zone boundary and improves agreement relative to the local dyadic model.

title: Three-Dimensional Impact Angle Control Guidance Law with Field-of-View Constraint
abstract: This paper presents a novel impact angle control guidance law to address the challenge of achieving any desired impact angle while satisfying the seeker's Field Of View (FOV) limit and maintaining acceleration continuity. The guidance problem is decomposed into two two-dimensional (2D) engagement planes. In the first plane, a pure proportional navigation guidance (PNG) law is employed toward a virtual target to align the missile velocity vector with the line-of-sight (LOS) to the target. In the second plane, a two-stage time-varying biased PNG (TVBPN) strategy is utilized to accurately shape the trajectory and achieve the desired terminal impact angle while maintaining compliance with FOV limitations. The position of the virtual target point ensures a smooth and continuous lateral acceleration at the transition between the first and second stages. The effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed law were validated through numerical simulations.

title: Borel combinatorics of $\mathbb{N}^{\ell}$-shift actions and hypersmooth equivalence relations
abstract: We conjecture that for each integer $\ell\geq 2$, the equivalence relation arising from the shift action of $\mathbb{N}^{\ell}$ on $2^{ω^{\ell}}$ is hypersmooth. We prove this conjecture for $\ell=2$, reduce the general case to a problem in Borel graph colorings, and establish the general case in measure. We also show that under certain mild hypotheses on a hypersmooth equivalence relation $E$, every finite-index Borel super-equivalence relation of $E$ is hypersmooth.

title: GNN-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Coastal Emergency Response under Extreme Water Levels
abstract: When a storm surge approaches a coastal town, the emergency plan must be put into action quickly using water-level forecasts, flood extent, road access, vulnerable residents and shelters. Bringing this information together under time pressure is slow and depends on the duty officer's expertise. This paper is one step in a wider research line from data to safe decisions: machine learning to understand the hazard, reinforcement learning and planning to choose actions, large language models (LLMs) to explain and cross-check them, and an assurance layer that keeps people in charge. Here we address the action step on a real place. We ask whether a policy can learn the timing of emergency actions from decades of real events. Lido di Venezia is represented as a heterogeneous graph built from public elevation, road, building and census data and driven by hourly tide-gauge records from 1983 to 2024, with seven actions taken from the municipal emergency plan. A PPO policy is trained on this graph and compared, on storm windows unseen in training, with a rule-based system simulating the officer's discretionary decisions. On 18 historical test scenarios, PPO achieves a similar reduction in population exposure to the rule. With uncertain forecasts and limited protection it again performs similarly but does not outperform the tuned rule, and removing graph message passing does not substantially reduce performance. PPO therefore learns an effective protective response from an outcome-based reward alone: it is given the plan's actions and when each is allowed, but not the thresholds that tell the comparator when to act. Next steps test harder edge cases, move closer to a digital twin of the territory, and replace the simulated officer with assessment by emergency-management stakeholders, supported by LLM-based interpretation of each recommendation.

title: Self-supervised learning for zebrafish embryo phenotype evaluation: Systematic comparison of algorithms, label-efficient classification, and transfer learning
abstract: Zebrafish embryos are a prominent model organism for image-based phenotyping and especially suited for large-scale imaging studies, for which machine learning (ML) models can automate evaluation. However, training ML models usually requires large labeled datasets, and differences in imaging conditions often impede reuse across laboratories. Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses both constraints by learning transferable representations from unlabeled images. Yet central aspects like the choice of algorithm remain underexplored for domain-specific applications. To close this gap, we benchmark popular SSL algorithms on the public EmbryoNet dataset, explore label-efficient learning, and test transfer to an unseen setting. Using representations from our strongest model, a ResNet50 network trained with SwAV, a simple linear classifier reaches 86.4% accuracy and a non-linear classifier 87.1%, rivaling the fully supervised EmbryoNet model (87.1%). The SwAV model decisively outperforms supervised training from scratch when labels are scarce (70.2% vs. 45.7% accuracy with 5% of labels). On a three-class problem (normal, dead, falsely cropped) with a small, previously unseen zebrafish toxicity dataset, recorded in a different setting, our model reaches 81.3% accuracy without retraining, while EmbryoNet achieves 75.9%. Overall, self-supervised models for zebrafish embryos seem to mostly facilitate label-efficiency and transfer to new settings rather than improving supervised results.

title: Ramsey sets are canonically Ramsey
abstract: A set $A$ of points is called Ramsey if, for each $r$, every $r$-coloring of a sufficiently high-dimensional Euclidean space contains a monochromatic congruent copy of $A$. We show that for each Ramsey set $A$, every $r$-coloring of a sufficiently high-dimensional Euclidean space, regardless of the number of colors used, contains a monochromatic or a rainbow congruent copy of $A$. This answers a question raised in virtually every paper on the topic.

title: ANNA: Attention-Free Neural Neighborhood Aggregation for Channel Estimation on Regenerative NTN Payloads
abstract: Accurate deep learning (DL)-based channel estimation (CE) for non-terrestrial network (NTN) uplinks must meet the processing, power, and latency constraints of regenerative payloads. We propose Attention-free Neural Neighborhood Aggregation (ANNA), a lightweight architecture combining per-resource block (RB) pilot projection, convolutional neighborhood aggregation, and shared reconstruction, with dense-grid expansion only at the output. Evaluation against learned and classical estimators uses paired waveform-generated datasets with receiver frequency correction enabled and disabled. With correction enabled, 16-bit floating point (FP16) deployment on a 10 W Jetson Orin NX achieves 0.372 ms 99th-percentile (P99) latency and 2.15 dB lower mean normalized mean-squared error (NMSE) than the fastest learned baseline at 29.6% higher latency. Relative to the most accurate learned baseline, ANNA is 4.08 times as fast and consumes 80.5% less module energy per sample, with a 1.14 dB accuracy penalty. It meets the adopted 0.5 ms P99 target in all 100 benchmark runs, demonstrating a favorable accuracy-latency-energy trade-off for embedded uplink CE.

title: Canonical metrics on punctured spheres, I: the mass matrix and the polygon model
abstract: A canonical metric $g_{\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}}$ on $S^n \setminus \mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$, where $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}=(p_1,\ldots,p_{\ell})$ and $n \ge 3$, is a metric conformal to the round metric that is complete, scalar-flat, and asymptotically flat at each puncture $p_i$. For $n=3$ these metrics are the Brill--Lindquist time-symmetric initial data for $\ell$ black holes, and their ends carry ADM masses. In this paper we study the masses, through the mass matrix, as functions on the conformal moduli space $M_{\ell}(S^n)$. The mass matrix $η=(η_{ij})$ is a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal and vanishing row sums (these matrices form the space $H_{\ell}$), and it determines the \emph{normalized ADM mass} at the $i$-th end via $\hat{\mathfrak{m}}_i=\sum_{j\ne i}e^{η_{ij}}$. We prove that the mass map $Ξ\colon M_\ell(S^n)\to H_{\ell}$ is a homeomorphism onto its image. On the other hand, the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_\ell(S^n)$ is homeomorphic to the moduli space of those equilateral $\ell$-gons in the hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^{n+1}$ whose sides, extended to infinity, end at distinct points (the Gauss map). By a theorem of Kapovich--Leeb--Millson and Balser, every polystable configuration is the Gauss image of such a polygon, and the Gauss map identifies the space of all equilateral $\ell$-gons with a natural compactification of $M_\ell(S^n)$. In particular, the mass matrix has an explicit description in terms of the pairwise vertex distances of the polygon. The mass matrix diverges as punctures collide. The degeneration, its renormalization, and the resulting compactification of the moduli space are the subject of a sequel to this paper.

title: DexFormer 2.0: Towards a Cross-Embodiment Foundation Policy for Dexterous Grasping
abstract: Dexterous grasping policies are usually trained for one arm paired with one hand. Every new pairing then needs its own policy, and the number of policies grows with every arm and hand added. We ask whether a single policy can control many arm-hand combinations and transfer to pairings and hands it has never seen. This is hard because robots differ in the number, layout, and dynamics of their joints, so their observations and actions share no common interface. We present DexFormer 2.0, a single reinforcement learning policy for cross-embodiment dexterous grasping. It maps every robot to a canonical joint interface with validity masks, encodes each joint's morphology with attention biased by the kinematic tree, and uses a Transformer-XL memory to infer embodiment-dependent dynamics from recent interaction. Trained on 18 combinations of four arms and six hands, it reaches 89% stable success on seen combinations and 51% on six held-out arm-hand pairs, outperforming GRU and DexFormer 1.0 baselines. Without fine-tuning, it also grasps with four new hand types and, through retargeting, with parallel grippers. Ablations show that memory, the kinematic-tree bias, and broader pairing coverage each matter for transfer. On a physical Flexiv arm, distilled students transfer zero-shot from simulation with two hands, including a held-out pair. Project website: https://davidlxu.github.io/dexformer2-web/.

title: Beyond AUC: Do Mammography Risk Models Predict When Cancer Occurs?
abstract: Longitudinal deep learning models for mammography-based breast cancer risk prediction output either per-year cumulative risks or a discrete distribution over the year of diagnosis, from which cumulative risks F1,...,F5 are derived. These models are evaluated almost exclusively with year-wise AUCs and the concordance index. We show that these metrics are largely insensitive to when cancer occurs: they can be high even for a model that carries no information about the year of diagnosis. We re-evaluate two recent longitudinal models (OA-BreaCR, LMV-Net) on CSAW-CC with a 5-year horizon using timing metrics computed on cancer cases only. Despite C-indices up to 0.75, neither orders cancer cases by time to diagnosis significantly better than chance (c_time 0.51 and 0.55, both 95% CIs covering 0.5). Weighted absolute timing error favours a constant "year 3" prediction over both models, so we use c_time as the primary timing metric. For Mirai's additive-hazard head, also used by LMV-Net, we analyse how per-year increments passed through a ReLU can collapse under severe class imbalance. We also propose a breast-level, two-stage model that separates whether from when. It matches LMV-Net in discrimination (C-index 0.745 vs. 0.746) but orders cancer cases better (c_time 0.58 vs. 0.51, paired 95% CI of the difference 0.01-0.13), on par with Mirai's published weights (0.57).

title: The Manifold-Index Model: provably and efficiently avoiding the statistical and computational curse of dimensionality
abstract: We study vector-valued regression with predictors filling a tube around an unknown $m$-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$ in $\mathbb{R}^D$. In the Manifold-Index Model, the mean response is $F=f\circΠ_{\mathcal{M}}$, where $Π_{\mathcal{M}}$ is the nearest-point projection onto $\mathcal{M}$ and $f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^p$ is a possibly non-injective link function. Multiscale ANisotropic lOcal Regression (MANOR) estimates tangent planes by multiscale PCA of predictors with similar responses, then refines them by pooling outer products of local slopes. The neighborhoods narrow tangentially while retaining complete normal fibers. We assume a Lipschitz link differential and bounded response noise. For $p\ge m$, under our geometric and sampling conditions, $n$ independent observations give mean tangent-space error of order $n^{-2/(m+4)}$ and integrated squared prediction error at the $m$-dimensional nonparametric rate $n^{-4/(m+4)}$, up to logarithmic factors. In a scaling regime with fixed intrinsic dimension, model and scale parameters, and ratio of manifold volume to the $m$-th power of its reach, the required sample size grows polynomially in $D+p$, and computation is polynomial in $n$, $D$ and $p$. Numerical experiments on curves with non-monotone links and surfaces with vector-valued responses compare observed convergence rates with the theoretical bounds; a Langevin dynamics example tests prediction of hitting probabilities under an approximate manifold-index model.

title: Medicaid Quality Disparities: Domain-Specific Performance Analysis and Approaches for State-Level Improvement
abstract: Medicaid covers nearly 78 million people, yet care quality varies across states, programs, and clinical domains. Using the 2024 CMS Child and Adult Core Sets (9,781 usable state-measure observations from 11,100 records), this study combined descriptive statistics, benchmark-gap analysis, correlation, and OLS regression to find where shortfalls cluster. Disparities were strongly domain-specific. Maternal and Perinatal Health scored lowest (28.0%), followed by Dental and Oral Health (38.5%) and Behavioral Health (44.4%), while Long-Term Services and Supports (82.8%) and Experience of Care (67.8%) scored highest. State performance correlated strongly with national benchmarks (r = 0.77, approximately), so rates should be read against each measure's benchmark. Domain was the strongest predictor, and the model explained 31.2% of variance. Because of heteroscedasticity and influential observations from mixing bounded and utilization measures, estimates are descriptive. Quality improvement should be targeted by domain, prioritizing maternal health, behavioral health network adequacy, and dental provider participation.

title: A Bleichenbacher bit-by-bit oracle attack from partial message knowledge
abstract: Oracle attacks show the importance of a correct implementation of cryptographic standards when translated into code. A notable example is the Bleichenbacher attack on RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding and all the improvements that have been suggested over the decades. This paper shows how an attacker knowing a few least significant bytes of an RSA message can take advantage of a server with an oracle side-channel to decrypt the full message bit by bit. We will consider two oracles that can be tested with chosen ciphertexts: one revealing whether the decrypted message starts with the 00 02 bytes and a second one revealing if the decrypted message is fully PKCS compliant. For an attacker knowing the three least significant bytes of the message, the first oracle provides an attack where one oracle call gives the next least significant bit of the message and the second an attack which requires, with high probability, a small constant number of oracle calls to the oracle, with a constant which depends on the length of the message and the desired probability of success. The attack divides the message bits into two sections, one with the known part and one with the unknown part, and then chooses transformations that will keep the unknown part, except for the last unknown bit, orders of magnitude below the integer coming from the known part. The resulting string either gives a valid padding or not depending on the value of the unknown bit. The attacker can minimize the number of oracle calls at the cost of some local computation. Finally, the same method is adapted to show how it can also be used to extract the few least significant bytes of the message with an increased cost where the main complexity is finding a second valid message with a correct padding starting from the original captured ciphertext.

title: Visual Marking as a Native Reasoning Capability for Multimodal LLMs
abstract: Visual reasoning often requires maintaining intermediate spatial states that are difficult to express in text. Existing approaches either rely on external drawing tools or image generators, or encode these states in latent tokens without explicit spatial correspondence to the input image. We introduce SelfMark, which enables MLLMs to construct and use visual marks directly in their native visual feature space. By treating the visual token grid as a canvas, SelfMark establishes explicit spatial correspondence between marks and images. This is achieved through a locate-mark-read procedure, where the model identifies relevant locations, constructs task-dependent mark features, and reads the resulting visual features to guide its reasoning. We jointly train a single model on spatial planning, dense counting, high-resolution VQA, and line tracing. Across six benchmarks, SelfMark outperforms state-of-the-art MLLM-based methods specialized for individual tasks. These improvements also persist with a stronger backbone, demonstrating the effectiveness of visual marking across different model capabilities. Overall, SelfMark provides a unified approach to visual reasoning by integrating spatially grounded marks directly into the visual feature space of MLLMs.

title: Functional Information, Optimal Channel Simulation and Lossy Source Coding
abstract: We characterize, within a constant number of bits, the minimum achievable rate for several one-shot coding problems, such as channel simulation and lossy source coding. The basis of our work is a new information measure between random variables $X, Y$ that we call the functional information $I_F(X \to Y)$. We show that this quantity characterizes the minimum one-shot rate $R^*(X \to Y)$ of channel simulation, in which a sample $Y \sim P_{Y \mid X}$ is communicated in the presence of common randomness: $I_F(X \to Y) \leq R^*(X \to Y) < I_F(X \to Y) + 1.45$. For the achievability result, we construct an explicit code using the Poisson functional representation. Using these results, we develop new bounds for one-shot variable-rate lossy source coding: given some distortion measure $Δ$, we use $I_F(X \to Y)$ to define the functional rate-distortion function $R_F$. Then, letting $R_O$ denote the one-shot operational rate-distortion function with private encoder randomness and distortion measure $Δ$, we make use of our channel simulation result to show that $R_F(D) \leq R_O(D) < R_F(D) + 2.45$ at every positive distortion level $D$. Finally, we generalize our channel simulation result by introducing the Rényi $α$-functional information $I_{F, α}(X \to Y)$ and show that it characterizes the minimum Arimoto-Rényi conditional entropy for channel simulation, ${R^*_α(X \to Y)}$, associated with the Campbell cost: ${I_{F, α}(X \to Y) \leq R^*_α(X \to Y) \leq I_{F, α}(X \to Y) + O(1/α)}$.

title: Pre-amplification for Preserving Quantum Resources Through an Open-Air, Room-Temperature Microwave Channel
abstract: We model a scenario where the pre-amplified signal mode of a two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) state generated by a Josephson parametric converter (JPC) is transmitted through a room-temperature, open-air channel, while the idler is retained at low temperature. Before transmission, the state contains three quantum resources: (1) entanglement, (2) non-classicality, and (3) sub-vacuum conditional prediction of the signal quadrature. To preserve these resources through noise and loss, we consider two forms of quantum-limited pre-amplification of the signal mode: phase-preserving amplification (PPA) and phase-sensitive amplification (PSA). We identify three thresholds for a fixed amount of loss as noise increases from zero marking the loss of (1) entanglement, (2) non-classicality, and (3) sub-vacuum conditional prediction of the signal quadrature, respectively. We find first that entanglement is fatally sensitive to the noise and loss in our channel model and neither form of pre-amplification protects it. On the other hand, phase-sensitive pre-amplification is shown to significantly raise the thresholds at which non-classicality and sub-vacuum conditional prediction are destroyed. For a 3-meter link between room-temperature horn antennas at 5 GHz, the noise thresholds for these resources can be orders of magnitude above the thermal background. Further analysis shows that these conclusions are robust to limited phase misalignment and pre-amplifier-added noise, with the latter having the stronger effect. These surviving non-classical resources may support quantum-enhanced sensing, illumination, and metrology protocols even in regimes where entanglement itself is destroyed. Our results suggest that protocols that exploit these quantum phenomena are the most likely to succeed in microwave applications.

title: Resolvent-based modeling of turbulent flow over multilayer compliant surfaces
abstract: Compliant coatings offer a passive approach to modifying near-wall turbulence and potentially reducing skin-friction drag, but high-fidelity exploration of the coupled parameter space is costly. We develop a two-way coupled resolvent-Galerkin framework for turbulent channel flow over finite-thickness, layered viscoelastic coatings. The fluid is modeled using the Navier-Stokes equations linearized about a turbulent mean state, while the solid is represented by a through-thickness Galerkin discretization of the elastodynamic equations. The solid response is condensed into a spectral surface-impedance operator at the fluid-solid interface. At $Re_τ= 180$, stiff panels approach the rigid-wall response, whereas more compliant panels modify the low-rank response associated with the near-wall cycle. A Reynolds-number study shows that panels with fixed nondimensional material stiffness can produce different responses depending on whether their thickness scales with inner or outer flow length scales. The influence of viscoelastic damping is examined across low- and high-frequency regimes, where stiffness-proportional damping alters the high-frequency fractional-energy distribution, while the low-frequency distribution remains relatively insensitive to damping. For multilayer panels, the fluid-facing material determines the interfacial wave speed, while the subsurface stiffness distribution modifies the panel's effective thickness. Temporal stability analysis identifies regions of parameter space where a steady harmonic response is relevant and regions where instabilities grow. Finally, a leading-order, covariance-based drag-estimation framework relates the coupled response to changes in the mean flow and to the estimated skin-friction drag. Together, these tools provide a basis for screening coating designs and selecting candidates for high-fidelity simulations and experiments.

title: Canonical metrics on punctured spheres, II: compactified moduli spaces of black holes
abstract: Let $g_{\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}}$ denote the canonical scalar-flat metric on $S^n\setminus \mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ introduced in Part~I, which for $n=3$ corresponds to the Brill--Lindquist initial data for $\ell$ black holes, and let $η\in H_{\ell}$ be its associated mass matrix. In this paper, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the metrics and the mass matrix $η$ as subsets of punctures collide. Such collisions cause every mass to diverge; if a cluster $A$ of black holes collapses at a relative scale $t$, the mass matrix satisfies $η=E(A)\ln(1/t)+O(1)$, diverging along an explicit ray $E(A)\in H_{\ell}$. For nested families of clusters, this degeneracy structure naturally organizes into a space of rooted trees. Subtracting the divergence gives a renormalized mass matrix which extends smoothly to every stratum of the Axelrod--Singer compactified moduli space $\overline{M}{}^{\,\mathrm{AS}}_\ell= \overline C_{\ell-1}(\mathbb{R}^n)/\mathrm O(n)$ and splits naturally into one mass matrix per vertex of the bubble tree. Geometrically, at each vertex carrying punctures the suitably rescaled metrics converge to a complete scalar-flat metric with the nodes filled in, adjacent such pieces being joined by Schwarzschild necks, and the renormalized matrix acting as its mass data. For $n=3$, the necks contain minimal spheres, which are common apparent horizons of the merging holes. At vertices bearing two holes, we determine on which side of the limiting horizon each node lies, and we formulate as a conjecture the resulting criterion for a neck to be a component of the outermost horizon. We also compare the mass lower bound of Part~I with the Riemannian Penrose inequality. Because the mass matrix is invariant under rotations of the bubbles, it lives on a Deligne--Mumford-type quotient of the compactification.

title: CiGS: Conduction in Gaussian Splats for Interior Temperature Field from Thermal Images
abstract: We present a method for inferring the interior temperature distribution of a solid object from registered multi-view visible-spectrum and thermal images, even when the thermal views cover only part of its surface. We formulate steady-state heat conduction as a Laplace boundary value problem and solve it with a direct boundary integral equation discretized over a point cloud: a Gaussian reconstruction of the visible-spectrum images supplies the boundary geometry, and the thermal images supply the boundary data. We do not build surface or volume meshes at any stage in our method. Instead, we sample collocation points from rendered depth without the pixels at depth discontinuities, and use a density subtraction that keeps the interior evaluation accurate up to the surface. The whole chain is differentiable, and we use it to recover the pose and depth of heating pipes, insulation defects, and the shape of cracks from thermal images. We validate our method through experiments on boundary value problems with Dirichlet-only and mixed Dirichlet and Robin boundaries, using synthetic and real captured data on scenes with challenging topology. These experiments show that our method matches analytical solutions and has better accuracy than FEM solvers.

title: Multi-seed information diffusion with varying reproduction
abstract: We define the $S_hR_k$-process that generalizes the notion of Hamiltonicity through the lense of information diffusion. We say that a graph is $S_hR_k$-infectable if it can be fully infected by transmission trees seeded by at most $h$ initial infections in which each infection leads to at most $k$ others; or, equivalently, if it can be exactly vertex-covered by at most $h$ trees of degree at most $k$. While determining $S_hR_k$ infectability is NP-hard in general, we argue fixed-parameter tractability when parameterised by treewidth. Additionally, we give computational experimental results comparing the performance of several natural heuristics for minimising the number of initial infections required to an optimal LP-based approach on several standard complex network models. We find that a uniformly random approach outperforms greedy heuristics based on degree or clustering.

title: Characterizing nonlocal Sobolev spaces as generalized Bessel potential spaces
abstract: In this paper, we study nonlocal Sobolev spaces $H^{ρ,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with $p \in (1,\infty)$, defined via a general class of nonlocal gradients $D^ρ$ associated with a kernel function $ρ$. As our main contribution, we establish three new equivalent characterizations of these spaces. First, we describe $H^{ρ,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ in terms of Fourier multipliers involving the symbol of the nonlocal potential associated with $D^ρ$. Second, we give a thorough functional analytic treatment of the nonlocal $ρ$-Laplacian $Δ^ρ$, which allows us to represent general nonlocal Sobolev spaces through its square root $(-Δ^ρ)^{1/2}$. Third, we show that $H^{ρ,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ coincides with the image $g_ρ* L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for a suitable convolution kernel $g_ρ\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, which confirms that these spaces are genuine potential spaces. These results generalize the well-known fact that, in the special case of the Riesz kernel, the resulting fractional Sobolev spaces coincide with the classical Bessel potential spaces. In this spirit, the present work can also be viewed as introducing a natural notion of generalized Bessel potential spaces.

title: Maximum likelihood degrees of 3D polytopes built from polygons of ML degree one
abstract: We construct 3D polytopes that admit a scaling with maximum likelihood (ML) degree one by using codimension zero toric fiber products of lower-dimensional polytopes and classify all the 3D polytopes that can be constructed in this way. We also study a family of 3D polytopes whose faces admit ML degree one scalings. We give a tight lower bound for the ML degree of these polytopes with a square base and we show that every value between this bound and the normalized volume of the polytope can be attained. These values depend on counting common and repeated roots associated to certain univariate polynomials. This is similar in spirit to the description of the possible ML degrees of rational normal scrolls.

title: Structural properties of semi-cutting sets
abstract: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph, let $T\subseteq V$, and let $F\subseteq E$. We call $F$ semi-cutting for $T$ if $d_{G}(u,w)<d_{G\setminus F}(u,w)$ for every two distinct terminals $u,w\in T$. We prove the sharp bound $|F|\ge |T|-1$. The argument is structural: semi-cutting sets are first identified with edge transversals of all shortest terminal-terminal paths, and the bound then follows from a contraction step, a terminal-deletion lemma, and a lexicographic induction on $(|T|,|V|)$.

title: Protecting Safety during Reasoning Training with Low-Rank Fisher Regularisation
abstract: Large language models are trained to have safety guardrails, but these can be compromised while fine-tuning for new capabilities, such as reasoning. One way to mitigate this degradation is to modify the fine-tuning objective to preserve safety behaviour, but doing so effectively and efficiently remains challenging. We revisit Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which penalises parameter updates based on sensitivity estimates from the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix (FIM). While EWC provides some protection, the diagonal approximation ignores interactions between parameters. We address this limitation by exploiting recent findings that safety-relevant behaviour is located in a low-rank subspace within models. Our method, Subspace-Projected Elastic Weight Consolidation (SP-EWC), projects gradients onto this subspace to capture non-diagonal curvature efficiently. We investigate three different ways of identifying the safety subspace: through safety fine-tuning updates (LoRA), safety-related activations (ActSVD), and contrastive representations of safety and utility data (cPCA). We find that this choice substantially affects performance, with SP-EWC using cPCA comparing favourably against existing methods by better maintaining safety guardrails without introducing excessive over-refusal.

title: Benchmarking LLM Inference on Desktop-Scale NVIDIA Grace Blackwell Clusters
abstract: Two NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 systems connect directly over 200 GbE to serve larger language models and increase inference capacity, but the benefits depend on how they are deployed. We benchmark 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, 8B to 235B parameters and four weight precisions on one and two RDMA-connected systems. Using vLLM, we compare tensor parallelism (TP=2), pipeline parallelism (PP=2) and a two-replica baseline at concurrency 1 to 64, with three independent launches per configuration. TP=2 delivers a median 1.59x peak-throughput gain over one Spark, versus 1.39x for PP=2 and has higher throughput in 93 of 96 matched comparisons with separated 95% Welch intervals. It reduces unloaded inter-token latency to 0.52x to 0.73x of one Spark, whereas PP=2 provides little reduction. TP=2 also achieves the highest goodput under a strict 100 ms inter-token latency objective wherever both strategies are supported and the objective is met. For models fitting on one Spark, TP=2 generally favors low-concurrency serving, while replication offers higher throughput at high concurrency. One Spark uses less GPU energy per output token at matched concurrency. Across three precision ladders, NVFP4 reduces unloaded latency more than adding a second Spark at BF16. NCCL microbenchmarks and comparisons with an earlier TCP campaign suggest that collective communication overhead contributes to the advantage of TP=2. These results provide deployment guidance for desktop-scale inference.

title: Geometric tracking of a halo CME using full-circle wide-field views from PUNCH
abstract: We tracked the large, geoeffective halo coronal mass ejection (CME) of 2025-May-31 across the very wide field of view of the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission, as a proof of concept for data-informed forecasting of CME arrival times at Earth. using simple point-and-click measurement of the front location as far as 47 degrees away from the Sun itself, we constrained an analytic "ludicrous ice-cream cone" geometric model with just three parameters: position angle, off-Earth-Sun angle, and propagation speed. We show that the model is sufficient to capture the bulk envelope of the CME, and also insufficient to capture the complexity of the CME's evolution. We generated simulated arrival-time forecasts for the CME by extrapolating the constant-velocity propagation to determine the time of impact with Earth. These "retro-forecasts" converged to within 30 +/- 15 minutes of the actual arrival time, 8 hours prior to arrival. The convergence was marked by a clear inflection point in the curve of predicted-arrival-time vs time-of-forecast. We conclude that continuous wide-field tracking is sufficiently powerful to enable even crude models to substantially improve arrival-time forecasting precision, and discuss future work required both to validate this single-event result and to extend it to more sophisticated analyses.

title: Where the Savings Go: The Limits of Hiding Cross-Tenant Cache Hits in LLM Serving
abstract: LLM serving engines cache prompt prefixes; a cache hit skips computation and returns faster, so a shared cache reveals whether others have sent a given text. Per-account salting closes this channel but forgoes cross-tenant reuse and isolates only whole accounts, even where access is redistributed or trust domains are subdivided below them. Defenses that share globally but hide hits promise reuse without relying on account boundaries. Hiding a hit requires everything tenants observe afterwards to be distributed as if it had missed. The defenses we examine target the hit-miss gap; we instead follow where the saved time goes. Step-based schedulers that never idle while work waits pass it in full to every request queued behind the hit, shifting each earlier by the same amount. An attacker within ordinary rate limits brackets a probe with two groups of listeners that each return one token, sends them in one short burst, and counts in how many steps they finish. Replaying a production trace on one vLLM instance at up to half capacity, a single probe detects cached texts of 256 tokens or more with advantage at least 0.98. Hiding only the hit request falls to one probe on vLLM and SGLang; random delays must reach about ten times the shift or more to cut the advantage to 0.1; narrowing what is shared gives no guarantee against this inference. Since any observable tenant benefit is also a signal, we prove that a rate-limited tenant's gain from content written by k other accounts is at most of order k times the leakage allowed, whatever the provider does with identities; at zero leakage, only the provider keeps the savings. Exact hiding is attainable in principle on one instance, but mechanisms that only pause or hold work know skipped work's duration only approximately, so under saturated prefill they must pad every step that may hold a hit, at a price that grows with time rather than with hits.

title: Causal Discovery for Resiliency-Prioritized Transmission Expansion Planning in Power Systems with Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources
abstract: Transmission planners at regional transmission organizations (RTOs), independent system operators (ISOs), and NERC-registered entities have limited analytical resources for exploring expansion options that improve resiliency for withstanding and recovering from fault conditions in electric power systems that are dominated by grid-forming (GFM) and grid-following (GFL) inverter-based resources (IBRs). Conventional existing TPL-001 contingency analysis will assess if a performance benchmark is violated. However, it will not identify which dynamic states and inputs caused the violation, nor how much a protective action will avoid propagation into a cascading outage. This paper proposes an analytical method that combines time-series causal discovery using the Peter and Clark Momentary Conditional Independence (PCMCI) algorithm with right/left eigenvector participation-factor analysis of validated small-signal state-space models. Synthetic data are generated from linearized models derived from substation phasor measurement unit (PMU) data. This includes node-breaker topologies under alternative transmission switching configurations. GFM and GFL inverter controls including phase-locked loops (PLLs) and fault ride-through logic. A planning index referred to as the Resiliency Causal Contribution Index (RCCI) is defined that weights PCMCI-derived causal effects on a TPL benchmark quantity by modal participation. The planning procedure iterates contingency categories, measures margins to RTO/ISO benchmarks for transient voltage recovery, oscillatory damping, inverter ride-through, and TPL-008-1 extreme temperature. The process infers automatic protective actions and repeats until a cascade is ruled out or confirmed. A simplified case study illustrates the entire process for considering the options in transmission expansion planning.

title: Model-Free Stealthy Attack on Vehicle Systems and Its Implications for ISO/SAE 21434 Risk Assessment
abstract: This paper investigates a model-free stealthy adversary targeting in-vehicle networks and its implications for automotive cybersecurity risk assessment. Conventional stealthy false-data-injection (FDI) attacks often assume privileged knowledge of system dynamics, estimator parameters, or detector statistics, understating the feasibility of adversaries with limited system information. We develop a model-free FDI attack that uses a Vector Autoregressive model with Exogenous inputs (VARX), identified from passively recorded nominal measurements, to characterize a compromised channel and construct attack sequences within a data-calibrated residual envelope. The construction requires no vehicle dynamics model, estimator parameters, assumed noise distribution, or detector knowledge. In a closed-loop lane-keeping benchmark, the attack induces a 1.25 m lateral displacement, exceeding the specified 0.9 m half-lane width, and keeps the vehicle outside the lane corridor for 9.21 s. At a matched 1 % false-alarm operating point, attack-period alarm rates stay below 2.4 % across five learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs), a chi-squared residual monitor, and a liveness monitor, versus 66-100 % for conventional baselines. The proposed adversary matches the impact and evasion of a privileged model-based adversary while requiring 13 fewer attack-potential points, raising its assessed feasibility from Low to High under the considered ISO/SAE 21434 Threat Analysis and Risk Assessment (TARA). We further show that conventional impact-and-feasibility risk scoring can assign identical risk to attacks with substantially different detector responses, and introduce a detection-conditioned risk formulation to distinguish them. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for adversarial knowledge requirements and measured detectability when assessing risks in safety-critical vehicle systems.
