For the metric equation \[ \partial_tg = -2\operatorname{Ric}_g + \frac12\mathcal K_{g,H}, \] we derive the corresponding bracket evolution \[ \dotμ= -π(P_{μ,H})μ, \qquad P_{μ,H} = \operatorname{Ric}_μ^{\sharp} - \frac14\mathcal K_{μ,H}^{\sharp}. \] We apply this formulation to the full flag manifold $\mathrm{SU}(3)/T^2$. For a prescribed closed invariant three-form, we compute explicitly the quadratic flux operator, the induced three-parameter metric system, and the evolution of the transported bracket coefficients. The system has exactly four positive stationary points. They correspond to the normal homogeneous Einstein metric and the three invariant Kähler--Einstein metrics. The normal stationary point has unstable index two, whereas each Kähler--Einstein stationary point has unstable index one. When the flux also evolves by the Hodge heat equation, we derive the closed system for its amplitude and the three metric coefficients. Every isotropic solution becomes extinct in finite time, with $h^2/λ^2\to0$. For a nonzero transverse mode the absolute perturbation is of order $(T-t)^{3/5}$, whereas the perturbation relative to the collapsing scale is of order $(T-t)^{-2/5}$. We relate the invariant three-form to the NS--NS sector of the strict $\mathrm{SU}(3)$-structure ansatz in type IIA supergravity.

title: Galaxy number counts in area distance space
abstract: We investigate how galaxy clustering changes when area distance is used as the radial coordinate. We derive the linear relativistic number counts for a flux-selected population and compare them with redshift and luminosity distance space. Source motion does not change the beam area at a fixed emission event, so area-distance clustering has no Kaiser distortion. Lensing changes both the angular and radial positions of sources, and can enhance area-distance clustering while weakening its correlation with redshift-space clustering. Observer motion shifts area-distance shells in the opposite direction to redshift and luminosity-distance shells, allowing their kinematic dipoles to point in opposite directions. A combination of the three count fields cancels their common intrinsic density and explicit evolution and magnification biases, leaving a signal dominated by velocities nearby and optical effects at larger distances. We relate this signal to galaxy-size magnification, so that its correlations can be inferred statistically without precise distances to individual galaxies.

title: A Second Order Transport Scheme for Dynamic Portfolio Subspaces under a Varying Risk Metric
abstract: We analyze the transport of portfolio exposures between moving subspaces under a varying positive definite risk metric. The reference evolution is the induced connection obtained from the ambient connection of minimum norm in fixed asset coordinates. An explicit expansion of risk weighted Procrustes identifies a leading local error that couples metric deformation with covariant motion normal to the subspace. A rank two construction with an exact continuous solution shows that this term can reduce global accuracy to first order even when the metric commutes with its derivative. Geometric mean alignment and a symmetric Procrustes construction cancel the term and yield reversible updates with second order global accuracy. We establish uniform error bounds on nonuniform partitions, characterize the cases in which the Procrustes defect vanishes, and distinguish discretization error from errors in estimated geometry. We also characterize the connection induced by principal square root whitening and its relation to the selected transport. Manufactured examples confirm the predicted defect and convergence rates. A historical geometry stress test then estimates the defect from preceding observations and finds that it predicts the subsequent separation between risk weighted Procrustes and both second order updates, while the two second order schemes remain much closer to each other. Portfolio comparisons separately evaluate target persistence, turnover, and economic implementation.

title: From Quasinormal Mode Poles to Branch Cuts at Finite $N$
abstract: In the strict large-$N$ limit, holographic thermal retarded correlators are typigcally meromorphic, with their late-time behavior determined by isolated quasinormal mode (QNM) poles. We show that the first bulk-loop correction, of order $1/N^2$, qualitatively changes this structure. In a scalar theory on the planar AdS$_5$ black brane, a one-loop bulk diagram generates poles at sums of two QNM frequencies at fixed loop momentum $q$; integration over the continuous momentum turns these QNM-pair poles into branch cuts. At vanishing external spatial momentum, for pairs built from QNM branches with opposite real parts, the leading light-cone contributions cancel at large momentum, and the residual QNM-pair frequency scales as $q^{-1/3}$. Consequently, an infinite family of cuts accumulates at zero frequency, while all tree-level QNM poles remain at finite nonzero frequencies. The first finite-$N$ correction therefore closes the gap set by the classical QNM spectrum. Competition between the decreasing QNM-pair damping and thermal Boltzmann suppression produces a moving saddle and a finite-$N$ contribution $G(t)\sim N^{-2}t^αe^{-Ct^{3/4}},\, C>0,$ which decays more slowly than the leading classical QNM contribution. Thus the large-$N$ expansion is nonuniform at late times, and bulk quantum fluctuations generate a distinct late-time regime beyond the classical QNM decay.

title: Palmprint Decomposer: Interpretable and Editable Factorization via Synthetic Learning and Instance-Wise Refinement
abstract: Palmprint recognition and synthesis methods focus on extracting discriminative textures or generating images with varied textures and appearances. However, they do not generally provide an explicit image-level representation that separates palmprint texture from its underlying base appearance for independent analysis or controlled editing. We introduce Palmprint Decomposer, an interpretable framework that represents a palmprint through independently editable factors and reconstructs the image through a multiplicative composition model. A color map and a light map characterize the base appearance, while a structure map and a global texture strength parameter describe texture modulation. However, accurate reconstruction alone does not guarantee separation of palmprint texture from base appearance, as fine palmprint textures may leak into the estimated base appearance. To mitigate this ambiguity, we train the decomposer exclusively on synthetic data with direct factor supervision, using asymmetric decoding paths and decomposition constraints to suppress texture leakage. Instance-Wise Refinement further improves real-image reconstruction by directly optimizing the predicted factors for each input without relying on the trained network. Experiments across seven datasets demonstrate high reconstruction fidelity, with the extracted structure maps generally achieving verification performance comparable to the original images. Compared with existing methods, our approach achieves better factor separation while preserving more discriminative palmprint texture information.

title: Analysis and Design of Spatially Coupled LDPC Codes for Pulsed-Jamming-Resilient Space Telemetry
abstract: Jamming is a major threat to space telemetry downlinks, which operate under severe power and bandwidth constraints. This paper develops a jamming-aware analysis and design framework for protograph-based spatially coupled low-density parity-check (SC-LDPC) codes. For pulsed jamming with jamming state information (JSI) at the receiver, we derive a two-state protograph-based extrinsic information transfer (PEXIT) recursion that tracks the messages originating from clean and jammed symbols separately and merges them at the check nodes through a mutual-information-matched Gaussian approximation. For non-interleaved pulsed jamming, we map each pulse realization, through the serialization of the lifted codeword, to a profile of jammed fractions over the variable-node types, and we prove that, under random lifting, this profile determines the local channel-state statistics. The resulting position-dependent thresholds are the objective of a constrained differential-evolution search over protographs, coupling memories, and edge spreadings. At different code rates, the designed ensembles are compared with the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) accumulate, repeat-by-4, and jagged accumulate (AR4JA) LDPC codes whose block length matches the SC-LDPC constraint length, with longer AR4JA codes whose block length is comparable with the size of the sliding window decoder, and with non-optimized SC-LDPC codes. Under pulsed jamming with random pulse positions and with JSI, the ensembles designed over random pulse realizations, decoded through sliding window decoding, reach a bit error rate of $10^{-4}$ at lower signal-to-noise ratios than all the benchmarks.

title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation
abstract: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

title: EviBridge: Encoding Predictive Visual Evidence for Proactive Interaction
abstract: Tool-handover interaction calls for preparation before a response is warranted. The model waits until interaction cues appear, then prepares while assessing whether the accumulating evidence supports a response or calls for cancellation. We introduce EviBridge, a framework that integrates predictive visual representations into a vision-language interaction model for joint state and tool prediction. A trainable evidence interface maps features from a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder into the language decoder alongside native visual inputs, preserving their temporal context and using only observations available at each decision time. The framework has two instantiations. EviBridge-E distinguishes recent from historical evidence and encodes the timing and spatial location of each observation. EviBridge-I preserves the temporal order of pooled V-JEPA 2 features and interaction turns and generates dedicated interaction tokens. We evaluate on FuGIBench, a streaming-video benchmark for preparation, response, and cancellation in tool-handover assistance. The best-performing variants of EviBridge-E and EviBridge-I achieve Overall scores of 0.6448 and 0.5892, compared with 0.2178 and 0.5327 for their respective task-adapted native baselines. These gains span target handovers, long waits, and cancelled requests, demonstrating the value of predictive visual evidence for interaction decisions.

title: The LAMOST Galaxy Parameter Catalog (LAGC): Stellar Populations, Kinematics, and Emission Lines of Galaxies in the LAMOST Spectroscopic Survey
abstract: The LAMOST Galaxy Parameter Catalog (LAGC) is a value-added data product of the LAMOST spectroscopic survey, generated by an automated spectral-fitting pipeline and released as a continuously updated catalogue series. Despite the vast data volume of the LAMOST spectroscopic survey, no dedicated, homogeneous pipeline had previously been able to extract stellar population, kinematic, and emission-line information simultaneously from its galaxy spectra, primarily because of the poorly controlled absolute flux calibration and a line spread function (LSF) that varies with wavelength, fibre, and time. The pipeline addresses both challenges through the SEW full-spectrum fitting method, which operates in equivalent-width space and is therefore immune to multiplicative flux-calibration errors, together with an accurate, wavelength-dependent model of the LAMOST LSF that enables unbiased kinematic measurements. As the pilot release of the catalogue series, we process the full galaxy sample of the latest LAMOST data release (283,691 spectra) and measure stellar population parameters, stellar and gas kinematics, and equivalent widths of 19 emission lines, each with bootstrap-based uncertainties. Repeat LAMOST observations confirm that the measurements are reproducible and that the bootstrap uncertainties are well calibrated, while comparison with SDSS shows only minor systematic offsets, attributable mainly to the SDSS LSF modelling. The measurements reproduce the well-established relations of the local galaxy population, and the catalogue will be publicly available and continuously updated as new observations become available. LAGC thus provides a reliable scientific catalogue for galaxy evolution studies, while the methodology behind it offers a blueprint for the next generation of fibre-fed spectroscopic surveys.

title: Model-free stiffness measurement of microscale soft contacts by far-field traction force microscopy
abstract: The microscale stiffness of soft materials governs their contact mechanics, adhesion and friction, yet it is surprisingly difficult to measure. Micro or nanoindentation is typically used, but extracting stiffness from these measurements requires using contact mechanics models (e.g. JKR), whose assumptions often break down for soft adhesive contacts. Here, we introduce far-field traction force microscopy (FF-TFM) to extract stiffness without using any contact model. We drag a colloidal probe mounted on an atomic-force microscope across a soft surface, measuring the friction force while imaging the displacements of fluorescent tracers on the substrate. Far from the contact, in the elastic limit, these lateral displacements depend solely on the friction force and the substrate stiffness, and fitting them with the point-force solution thus gives the substrate's Young's modulus directly. We successfully match bulk rheology moduli with FF-TFM for six different silicone elastomers, where JKR fits to indentation data underestimate moduli by as much as 40\% of their bulk values. Our approach also enables tracking how the probe slips across the surface. We find that soft contacts can "pre-slip" with no detectable signature in the force signal, unlike stiffer contacts. FF-TFM thus offers a contact-model-free route to measuring microscale stiffness and slip behavior in soft materials.

title: Cosmological Collider Signals from Fermion Bubble Loops with a Chemical Potential
abstract: We present the first systematic analytical calculation of the local and nonlocal cosmological collider (CC) signals generated by massive fermion bubble loops in the presence of an effective chemical potential during inflation. Working in the de Sitter approximation, we investigate the four-point correlator of inflaton perturbations in the single-squeezed limit. By combining CC cutting rules, late-time expansions, and partial Mellin-Barnes (MB) techniques, we derive analytical expressions for both local and nonlocal signals. In particular, we identify two distinct contributions to the local signal, arising from spectrum and integer poles and from ultraviolet poles of the loop-momentum integral. We further investigate the three-point limit, where the separately extracted local and nonlocal contributions develop apparent folded singularities. By reorganizing the MB representation, we demonstrate that these singularities cancel in the complete signal and obtain a convergent double-MB integral suitable for numerical evaluation. Independent calculations using complementary MB representations provide nontrivial consistency checks of our results. We find that the chemical potential can significantly enhance the oscillatory signal while increasing its logarithmic oscillation frequency. Our analytical results provide a foundation for further studies of chemical-potential-enhanced fermionic CC signals, including fermion triangle loops.

title: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation modulates auditory-evoked responses and conflict adaptation in humans
abstract: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) engages ascending neuromodulatory systems, and animal studies have motivated the hypothesis that it shifts sensory cortical processing toward feedforward (FF) relative to feedback (FB) transmission. Whether transcutaneous auricular VNS (taVNS) produces a corresponding pattern in humans remains unclear. In a single-blind, sham-controlled crossover study, 11 healthy adults received 120 min of taVNS (25 Hz, left tragus) and sham stimulation (left earlobe) in separate sessions. Click-evoked EEG was recorded before, twice during, and immediately after stimulation. Sensory discrimination thresholds and conflict adaptation in a Simon task were assessed before and during stimulation. Relative to Sham, taVNS attenuated the decline in the early P0 response across the session and enhanced the Pa-Nb response early during stimulation. The later P2 response did not show the increase observed under Sham. After stimulation, taVNS reduced click-locked theta (5-8 Hz) inter-trial phase coherence relative to Sham, with no significant between-condition difference in the change in theta power. Conflict adaptation increased under taVNS, whereas sensory thresholds and the overall Simon effect did not differ significantly between conditions. In exploratory analysis, greater decreases in theta phase coherence were associated with greater increases in conflict adaptation. These findings indicate that taVNS modulates auditory responses across processing stages and conflict-related behavior. The pattern is compatible with altered FF/FB weighting, but the direction of information flow and the underlying neuromodulatory mechanisms were not measured directly.

title: Life-cycle structural reliability of RC bridge piers under corrosion in a changing climate
abstract: Aging and deterioration processes of structures and infrastructure systems can be severely affected by the long-term evolution of environmental conditions expected in a changing climate. This paper aims at investigating the interaction between climate change and environmental aggressiveness on the probabilistic life-cycle performance of concrete structures under corrosion. A simulation-based framework is proposed for life-cycle structural reliability analysis under climate change scenarios. The framework is applied to a bridge pier with hollow core cross-section exposed to chloride-induced corrosion. The results allow to quantify the impact of climate change on long-term probabilistic structural response and highlight the need for proper modeling of the environmental parameters and climate evolution over the entire lifespan of aging structures for optimal life-cycle maintenance and management of structural and infrastructural facilities.

title: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
abstract: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.

title: Linear Algebra over Bands
abstract: We introduce Eckmann-Hilton operators on bands, which allow for a suite of matroidal constructions, in particular, matroid unions and matroid stable intersections. This enables the construction of general linear monoids over bands. Geometrically, we show that matroid stable intersection extends the transverse intersection of linear spaces over fields and the stable intersection of tropical linear spaces, lending new insight into intersection theory on bands.

title: Navital Gym: Rule-Graded Agent Environments for Indian Workflows
abstract: AI agents are being deployed on Indian workflows such as payments, tax, forms, travel and customer support in Hindi and Hinglish. Public agent evaluations rarely cover these workflows, and many score with another language model. We present Navital Gym, a set of six open environments with 321 public tasks in five task families: trip planning, UPI payments and disputes, GST invoicing and returns, form filling (including a multi-document split) and customer support in Hindi, Hinglish and three experimental Indian languages. Every task is graded by named, deterministic rules that recompute the outcome from a synthetic sandbox world. No language model judges any score. We report one run per task for three models on all six environments, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and for Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite on two (UPI and the Support core). Opus solves 315 of 321 tasks, Sonnet 302 and Haiku 205. Trip planning and Hindi/Hinglish support separate the models most. We also describe a private held-out set that is not published, and a 7B adapter trained in the gym. Code is Apache-2.0 and task data is CC BY 4.0. The rules are a documented simplification of Indian practice, not the live systems.

title: Improving Radio SLAM via Information Sharing: Collaborative Performance Bounds
abstract: This paper studies the fundamental performance limits of radio-based collaborative simultaneous localization and mapping (C-SLAM) in dense vehicular environments towards the 6G integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) era. We consider a collaborative estimation task consisting of multiple user equipments (UEs) with unknown local state variables together with joint estimation of unknown states of the environment landmarks or targets, using cellular radio measurements. Specifically, a posterior Cramér-Rao bound (PCRB) is derived for such centralized multi-UE cellular radio SLAM with information sharing, capturing the effects of the number of involved UEs, their geometric configuration, and their mutually different abilities to measure or observe different landmarks. The analysis reveals how information sharing scales with UE density, identifies regimes of diminishing returns, and provides estimator-independent limits for collaborative radio-based environment mapping and localization. The provided numerical results validate the proposed framework in a vehicular system context, while also demonstrating substantial gains against more ordinary single-UE radio SLAM approach.

title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
abstract: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

title: LEDGER: Auditable Agent Memory Under Change
abstract: Agent memory systems are mostly evaluated on fixed histories, and only their final answers are scored. In real use, facts change, sources differ in reliability, and users ask the agent to forget things. We present LEDGER, a memory layer in which a language model proposes facts and explicit rules decide which value is current, which source to trust, and what to delete. Each fact keeps its source and the period in which it held. LEDGER+EP adds a search over raw conversation turns for questions the ledger does not cover, and scrubs these turns on deletion. We compare both against no memory, full-history replay, retrieval over raw transcripts, and Mem0, with the same answering model and prompt, on a synthetic multi-session coding-agent workload and a 210-question subset of LongMemEval, and we score both the evidence each memory sends to the model and the answer. On the coding workload, LEDGER+EP in fallback mode answers 94.3% of questions correctly on five development seeds and 91.1% on five held-out seeds, against 82.1% and 83.3% for full replay, the strongest baseline. When a deletion request only describes the fact, no deleted value reached our systems' evidence in any evaluated probe. On LongMemEval, LEDGER+EP in augment mode has the same observed accuracy as full replay (74.8%) with 1% of its context. The main limitation is that the coding workload is synthetic and built by us; on LongMemEval, the differences between the strongest systems are within the confidence intervals.

title: Recovery of accidental bound states in the continuum in vertically asymmetric photonic lattices through radiation-source parity restoration
abstract: Vertical asymmetry generally precludes accidental bound states in the continuum (BICs) in planar photonic lattices, yet the underlying physical mechanism remains unclear. In this study, we show that accidental-BIC formation is governed by the definite parity of the transverse radiation-source profile rather than by geometric vertical mirror symmetry. A semianalytical coupled-mode analysis shows that an accidental BIC occurs when the radiation overlap integral of a leaky Bloch mode vanishes. We decompose the overlap into contributions from the even- and odd-parity components of the transverse radiation-source profile. Complete radiation suppression requires both contributions to vanish simultaneously. In vertically symmetric lattices, the source profile has definite even or odd parity, causing one contribution to vanish identically. Thickness tuning can null the remaining contribution and produce an accidental BIC. In vertically asymmetric lattices, by contrast, both parity components are generally present. The waveguide dispersion forbids their simultaneous vanishing, thereby precluding an accidental BIC. Introducing a parity-restoring layer into a vertically asymmetric lattice restores definite parity to the transverse radiation-source profile, thereby enabling the formation of an accidental BIC. Finite-element simulations confirm the analytically predicted recovery of accidental BICs for both TE$_0$ and TE$_1$ Bloch modes.

title: Transferable Neural CBFs via Generalized Closure
abstract: Classical control barrier functions (CBFs) provide safety constraints for controllers, but designing them by hand is difficult for underactuated vehicles and the resulting safe sets can be overly conservative. Neural CBFs can learn more informative barriers from data, yet a learned barrier is usually verified only for one fixed obstacle configuration. We study whether one neural barrier can be reused across environments by expressing the state relative to each obstacle. The key gap is that these relative coordinates may discard information needed to predict their own evolution. We give a generalized closure condition that represents this missing information as a residual and a lifting theorem that transfers a verified relative-coordinate barrier to every obstacle in a family. A rank test also identifies when symmetry alone cannot justify the transfer. We validate the conditions on a double integrator, a planar aircraft, and a 12-state quadrotor. Coordinates that fail the test lead to obstacle penetration or to a barrier condition that fails near hover, whereas body-frame coordinates close exactly for the quadrotor. The resulting barrier transfers to new maps without retraining and is effective in the reported deployment and fast-start experiments.

title: Affine pairs of minimizing units in totally real non-Galois cubic fields
abstract: Let $Γ$ be a rank-two subgroup of the integral norm-one units in a totally real non-Galois cubic field. We prove that two distinct affinely equivalent minima of Godwin's spread on $Γ\setminus\{1\}$ generate $Γ$ and determine its complete minimum set: a pair with sum $\pm2$ or a triple of integral translates of product one. Every minimum generates the order $\mathbb{Z}[Γ]$. For an order whose norm-one units have such a pair, the order generated by its units is the smallest suborder with the same minimum value. We also give explicit families and a maximal order with minima in two distinct affine classes.

title: Delay-induced anomalous density-polarization relation in chiral active matter
abstract: Aligning active matter can spontaneously exhibit diverse forms of ordered collective motion, and higher local density is generally expected to enhance local polarization. Meanwhile, delays in agents' responses are widespread in real active systems, raising the question of how delayed alignment affects collective motion and, in particular, whether higher local density still strengthens polar order. Here, using a chiral active particle (CAP) model with delayed alignment, we uncover a counterintuitive anomalous density-polarization relation (DPR) within droplets: the local polarization first increases and then decreases with increasing local density. Analysis of the deviation-angle dynamics reveals a delay-induced supercritical discrete Hopf bifurcation. Noise-sustained oscillations before the bifurcation and self-sustained oscillations afterward broaden the deviation-angle distribution and reduce polarization. Increasing the delay shifts the bifurcation to lower densities, enhancing the anomalous DPR in agreement with simulations. Using the nonequilibrium landscape-flux theory, we further identify the nonequilibrium flux as the dynamical origin of the anomalous DPR. Our findings not only establish time delay as a control knob for collective behavior in chiral active matter, but also offer a useful analytical perspective on anomalous density-order relations in other nonequilibrium systems exhibiting collective order.

title: Variational Corrections to Strong-Disorder Renormalization in the Two-Dimensional Random Transverse Field Ising Model on Quantum Hardware
abstract: Strong-disorder renormalization-group (SDRG) methods provide an effective description of disordered quantum many-body systems by identifying the dominant couplings for the low energy physics. However, the resulting renormalization-group flow is approximate and neglects correlations beyond the RG description. Here, we investigate whether variational quantum optimization can be used to correct these approximations. Building on the emergent-coupling-based ansatz (ECBA) developed for the one-dimensional random Heisenberg model, we introduce a formulation adapted to the two-dimensional random transverse field Ising model. The SDRG flow determines the structure of the circuit, while variational optimization allows the state to deviate from the RG approximation. We study the resulting ansatz numerically and experimentally on an IQM superconducting quantum processor. For a 16-qubit system, we perform full variational optimization on the quantum processor, while a 49-qubit system is investigated using pre-optimized parameters, achieving a relative energy accuracy of 89% and 97%, respectively. Our results demonstrate that RG information can be translated into shallow, hardware-compatible quantum circuits while variational optimization enables corrections beyond the underlying RG approximation also for two-dimensional systems.

title: Convergence rates of moment--SOS hierarchies with correlative sparsity via gluing and projection
abstract: This paper studies convergence rates of moment--SOS hierarchies with correlative sparsity. Following the method proposed in~\cite{tran}, we bound the Hausdorff distance between the set of sparse truncated moment sequences and sparse truncated pseudo-moment sequences. The central step is a quantitative gluing lemma on a clique tree: local moment errors and separator discrepancies in total variation control the error of a joint approximating measure. Over hypercube, polynomial kernels give the convergence rates $O((\log_2r)^3/r^2)$ for the correlative sparse quadratic module and $O(r^{-2})$ for the correlative sparse preordering, where the certificate degree is $2r$. On compact basic semialgebraic sets, slack variable lifting and global atom projection yield $O((\log_2r)^{3\Lo/2}/r^{\Lo})$ and $O(r^{-\Lo})$ with a Łojasiewicz exponent $0<\Lo \le1$. These bounds hold for fixed-degree Hausdorff distances and polynomial objective gaps. We also extend to result to the correlative sparse quadratic-module rate for scalar objectives with clique-local polynomial matrix constraints.

title: XRISM/Xtend detection of solar wind charge exchange induced by multiple coronal mass ejections in 2024 August
abstract: Solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) emission is often a major component of the soft X-ray background, but it also provides a remote diagnostic of the composition and ionization state of solar wind plasma. We present an analysis of a SWCX event observed with XRISM/Xtend during 2024 August 9-13. The event occurred during intense solar activity with multiple flares, including an X1.3-class solar flare, and associated coronal mass ejections (CMEs). We found a clear enhancement in the 0.3-3.0 keV count rate that occurred nearly simultaneously with an increase in the solar wind proton flux measured by ACE. We fitted the spectrum during the enhancement period with a set of Gaussian emission lines. In addition to the commonly detected C, N, and O lines, we detected Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe lines at $>15σ$ significance. We extracted two characteristic periods within the enhanced interval based on the CME arrival timeline. The O$_{\rm VIII}$/Si$_{\rm XIII}$ line ratio changed significantly between the two periods, suggesting contributions from multiple CME components. We then applied the AtomDB charge exchange model with a multi-temperature setup. The estimated ionization temperatures for Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe increased with the peak soft X-ray flux of the associated solar flares. This trend suggests that coronal heating becomes more efficient for more intense flares. Meanwhile, the ionization temperatures were lower than typical flare electron temperatures, implying that CME plasma may have been released into interplanetary space under non-equilibrium ionization conditions. We also found an indication of an inverse-FIP pattern, with reduced relative abundances of Si and S. These results demonstrate that XRISM/Xtend can diagnose the coronal plasma through SWCX emission, including heavy ions such as Ne, Mg, and Si, which are difficult to measure with current in-situ instruments (e.g., ACE satellite).

title: Razavi-Bench: Tracking AI Progress in Analog Circuit Reasoning
abstract: We propose Razavi-Bench, a benchmark built from the 50 questions in Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and graded by GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics, and use it to track how fast AI models improve at analog circuit analysis. Across 73 multimodal large language models released between May 2024 and November 2026, the top score rose from 28.83% to 98.33% in 30 months, mostly before the reference answers were published. The leading models now answer almost every textbook question correctly; the hardest questions show a circuit that resembles a textbook one but works differently, or ask about behavior the obvious analysis misses. Within two and a half years, a set of questions that exposed the limits of AI models has become one they answer almost perfectly.

title: ReAccess: Look Once, Stay Focused with Efficient Test Time Memory
abstract: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.

title: Learning What the True Labels Would Teach: Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning with Unlabeled Data
abstract: In class-incremental learning with unlabeled data, each task brings only class names and unlabeled images, so CLIP's zero-shot predictions replace labels. Existing methods train on hard pseudo-labels, but a wrong one gives the true class zero probability, which self-training often confirms. We argue that each image should carry its label posterior, as an analytic classifier trained on posteriors equals the true-label one in expectation. The zero-shot prediction is not this posterior, as its class proportions confound name bias with true imbalance and it ignores other images. We propose Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning (PACIL), which corrects the class prior with a prior selection rule and refines each distribution by a fixed-prior von Mises-Fisher mixture on whitened features. These soft labels train the classifier and replace labels to select its fusion weight with zero-shot CLIP by closed-form leave-one-out cross-validation. We prove that posterior targets minimize the mean-square gap to the true-label prediction and that their argmax widens this gap only through ambiguous images. The fusion weight selected with soft labels loses at most their distance to the posteriors in expected correct decisions. PACIL has the best average incremental accuracy among methods trained without labels on all 18 settings.

title: A consistent (3D) EFT expansion of the bubble nucleation rate. Part I: scalar theories
abstract: Precise predictions of bubble nucleation are essential for connecting cosmological phase transitions to their potential observational signatures. In this first paper of a two-part series, we develop a general, fully perturbative framework for incorporating higher-dimensional operators (HDOs) into nucleation calculations in scalar high-temperature effective field theories. Our approach consistently includes their effects on the bounce and the fluctuations around it, including interactions with higher derivatives. We prove that the resulting statistical rate is invariant under field redefinitions, and establish sufficient conditions for the existence of the perturbative bounce solution in the presence of HDOs. We illustrate the framework by applying it to a model containing a scalar and a fermion, where we find modest HDO corrections in its regime of moderately strong transitions. We thus extend the systematic study of HDO effects beyond critical thermodynamics and provide a controlled method for determining their impact on bubble nucleation.

title: TacBridge: Learning Unified Tactile Representations through Cross-Sensor Correspondence
abstract: Optical tactile sensors record tactile videos that capture local deformation and its temporal evolution during contact, supporting robot manipulation, force estimation, and tactile representation learning. Differences in imaging geometry, background appearance, illumination, resolution, and deformation response lead to sensor-dependent observations of the same contact across GelSight, DIGIT, GelSlim, TacTip, and other optical tactile sensors. This variability limits representation transfer and the joint use of multi-sensor data. We introduce TacBridge, a framework for learning unified representations from multi-sensor tactile videos through cross-sensor correspondence. Specifically, multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training learns spatiotemporal representations across sensors. We then train the same masked model jointly on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction, using paired source and target videos of matched contact events. Experiments on cross-sensor translation and downstream perception demonstrate the cross-sensor generalization and task transferability of the learned tactile representations.

title: Gravitational Potential of CALIFA Galaxies from the Blue Cloud to the Red Sequence
abstract: We explore the gravitational potential of 238 (E1$-$Sdm) CALIFA galaxies from the Blue cloud to the Red Sequence using the star formation rate$-$stellar mass diagram ($\mathrm{SFR}-M_\star$) diagnosis. On average, galaxies in the Blue cloud possess slow-rising circular velocity curves (CVCs), those in the Green valley have flat CVCs, while galaxies in the Red sequence are characterised with peaked CVCs. Both the maximum circular velocity ($V_{c,\mathrm{max}}$) and asymptotic circular velocity ($V_{c,\mathrm{flat}}$) of the galaxies increase from the Blue cloud to the Red sequence, and show approximately linear relations with the logarithmic offsets from the star-forming main sequence ($Δ\mathrm{SFR}$s). The $Δ\mathrm{SFR}-\log_{10}(V_{c,\mathrm{max}})$ relation has a steeper slope ($-0.154 \pm 0.012$) than the $Δ\mathrm{SFR}-\log_{10}(V_{c,\mathrm{flat}})$ relation ($-0.124 \pm 0.011$). These results suggest that $V_{c,\mathrm{max}}$, tracing the inner gravitational potential, indicates a stronger variation along the quenching parameter $Δ\mathrm{SFR}$ than $V_{c,\mathrm{flat}}$, which is more strongly influenced by the outer mass distribution and dark matter halo.

title: Vanishing geodesic distance phenomenon and boundedness of curvatures
abstract: This article concerns a conjecture proposed by Michor and Mumford in their 2005 paper, in which the vanishing of the geodesic distance is associated to the local unboundedness of the sectional curvature. In this article, we consider a Riemannian Banach manifold with all of its curvature tensors locally bounded. We derive several properties regarding the local boundedness of curvature tensors, and give a sufficient condition for a non-degenerate geodesic distance, which partially verifies the conjecture in its converse form.

title: vividRGB: Various visual cue detection in RGB photographs with forced focused attention
abstract: Natural photographs contain dense, overlapping structures that can be weakly expressed in feature maps from whole-image vision encoders. We introduce forced focused attention (FFA) and its Python implementation, vividRGB. FFA is an encoder-agnostic inference-time procedure that applies a frozen encoder to enlarged, overlapping local crops, averages inverse-aligned reflections, and reconstructs a feature field in source coordinates. We evaluate 50 high-resolution photographs from grassland vegetation, fungal networks, airborne forests, coral reefs, and phytoplankton microscopy, using DINOv3 ViT-B/16. Across the five domains, FFA at 5% or 10% focus produces higher mean RGB-edge boundary F1 than direct DINOv3 encoding and automatic SAM3 masks. Domain means range from 0.244 to 0.596 for FFA, versus 0.028-0.076 for direct DINOv3 and 0.020-0.090 for SAM3. Qualitative feature maps also show finer appearance structure. These results concern RGB-edge preservation rather than verified species, traits, or biological segmentation. Narrower focus generally improves boundary preservation, while extraction time and GPU energy use increase sharply and gains diminish at finer settings. FFA may be useful for relatively small, high-resolution ecological image collections where dense visual cues matter. The alpha release vividRGB 0.1.0 and versioned research resources support reproducible cue inspection.

title: From Strong Normalization to WhatsApp: the Journey of an Axiom
abstract: Twenty years ago, Mariangiola Dezani-Ciancaglini, Daniele Varacca and I showed that Milner's classic encoding of functions into processes does not respect one of the laws of intersection types, the one stating that $(σ\toτ)\land(σ\toρ)$ is a subtype of $σ\to(τ\landρ)$, which Barendregt, Coppo and Dezani-Ciancaglini had stated in 1983 for their filter $λ$-model. In this essay I show that this observation is the key to closing what a colleague at Meta calls ``the main typing gap in Erlang''---the language in which the servers of WhatsApp are written: the type of the function that implements a server is not related to the type of the server, so that a client may expect from the server a reply that the server will never send. Actually, closing this gap is just an excuse to follow the journey of the law above, and of some of its relatives, from the study of strong normalization in the $λ$-calculus to the type systems of Elixir and Erlang: a journey that shows how much the practical typing of these languages owes to the work of Mario Coppo, Mariangiola Dezani-Ciancaglini and Simona Ronchi Della Rocca, to whom this essay is dedicated for their eightieth birthdays.

title: Polymorphism and crystal suppression in symmetric mixtures with entropic interactions
abstract: We investigate the phases of a binary mixture of hard spheres with equal diameter and negative non-additivity, favoring hetero-coordination in dense samples. By performing extensive swap Monte Carlo simulations, we show that in an interval of small non-additivities, close to the eutectic point, the mixture fails to crystallize and the compressed fluid gets stuck in an amorphous state. The onset of glass at intermediate compositions is associated with the competition between FCC and B2 (CsCl-type) crystal structures. As the propensity of particles to hetero-coordinate grows further, however, the B2 crystal gives way to a B1 (NaCl-type) crystal at equimolarity, and again the mixture orders for all compositions. We argue that this happens because of the underlying FCC symmetry of the B1 crystal. These results, pertaining to a model with excluded-volume interactions only, point to the key role of entropy in generating amorphous structures in multi-component metallic, inorganic, and soft-matter glass formers.

title: Metrological Channels Induced by Encrypted Quantum Cloning: Optimal-Probe Fisher-Information Broadcasting and Single-Use Operational Recovery
abstract: Encrypted quantum cloning creates multiple individually inaccessible signal systems from which an unknown input state can be recovered by combining any selected signal with a shared quantum key. Here we study parameter estimation when a local sensing transformation is applied after encrypted cloning and before decryption. For the two-clone qubit protocol, a local Pauli rotation on one encrypted signal is shown to induce, after standard decryption, a parameter-dependent Pauli dephasing channel rather than a unitary rotation. We derive its Pauli-transfer representation and the corresponding quantum Fisher information (QFI) for arbitrary mixed qubit probes. We then distinguish raw QFI, which for an optimal decoded probe may remain simultaneously present in a decoded output and its complement, from decoder-accessible QFI, which is operationally single-use because a first decryption destroys the shared syndrome information needed for a second standard recovery. For $n\geq2$ encrypted clones, the effective channel family is independent of clone number up to a clone-parity-dependent permutation of the Pauli axes (the single-clone case is exceptional for $Y$-sensing, where the decoded map stays unitary). This produces a metrological parity switch: for fixed probe and generator, even and odd clone numbers can yield respectively vanishing and maximal QFI. Closed expressions are obtained for the degradation of this parity contrast under probe depolarization and Pauli-diagonal Bloch-vector contraction.

title: Dynamical theory of the East model. I. A review on the Zwanzig-Mori projection-operator formalism
abstract: The East model is a paradigmatic kinetically constrained spin model in one dimension that exhibits glassy dynamics. This review surveys the progress on the theoretical description of the dynamics of the East model, focusing on the spin time correlation function and the relaxation time. We summarize rigorous results on the super-Arrhenius scaling of the relaxation time in the low-temperature limit. We then present a unified derivation of the Zwanzig-Mori projection-operator formalism for both the fluctuation and domain bases. Within this formalism, an infinite hierarchy of coupled equations for the time correlation function and memory kernels emerges---a structure reminiscent of generalized mode-coupling theory developed for supercooled liquids. We review the analytical approximations obtained by truncating or closing the hierarchy at first or second orders and compare them against Monte Carlo simulations. Although these approaches perform reasonably at moderate temperatures, they universally fail in the low-temperature regime: mode-coupling closure schemes in the fluctuation basis introduce spurious ergodicity-breaking transitions, while truncations in the domain basis discard slower modes and fail to capture the asymptotic divergence of the relaxation time. The loss of analytical tractability beyond second order remains the central obstacle, underscoring the fundamental difficulty of describing hierarchical relaxation even in this ``simplest'' model of glassy dynamics.

title: List colouring of circular-arc graphs
abstract: A circular-arc graph takes a set of nonempty closed arcs on a circle as its vertex set, and two vertices are adjacent when their corresponding arcs intersect on the circle. We show the chromatic number of any circular-arc graph equals its list chromatic number. Our methodology is an application of Schauz's coefficient formula within the Alon-Tarsi and Combinatorial Nullstellensatz framework.

title: One Code per Material: Neural Representation and Generation of Measured BTFs
abstract: Measured bidirectional texture functions (BTFs) capture the full appearance of real materials--including parallax, self-shadowing and inter-reflections that analytic SVBRDFs cannot express--but each measurement is billions of values, and every new material requires a new capture. Existing neural BTF representations encode each material as large per-texel latent maps rather than as a point in a shared space from which new materials could be sampled. We present neural representations of measured BTFs at two operating points. A per-material coordinate network outperforms the recent neural BTF of Xia et al. at matched size (+3.2 dB PSNR) and all prior baselines on every metric. A compact model represents each material by a single 256-dimensional code that conditions a shared decoder; it exceeds the PSNR (+1.2 dB) and colour accuracy of the per-texel latent maps of Rainer et al. with 256 numbers per material instead of millions, and one decoder shared by all materials. Because each material is a single point in this code space, measured BTFs can be sampled: a class-conditional flow over the codes, trained on the 84 materials enlarged with colourways and hue rotations, generates materials that render and relight as full BTFs.

title: Multimodal assessment of the skin biomechanical properties during wound healing and hyaluronic acid response
abstract: Various methods such as elastography or mechanical testing have been developed to quantify the mechanical properties of soft tissues, which are related to the tissue local pathophysiological conditions. This study is the first one to investigate the in vivo performances of the Impact-Based Analysis Method (IBAM) to characterize the biomechanical behavior of skin during physiological mechanisms. A murine model (12 Sprague-Dawley rats) was considered and various measurements of skin mechanical properties were conducted on different regions of interest over a 3-week period. The effects of wound healing after full-thickness excisional wound and an intradermal hyaluronic acid (HA) injection were monitored using IBAM, as well as two commercially available devices: Cutometer__ and MyotonPro__. The indicators $Δ$t (from IBAM), R0 and R5 (from Cutometer__) vary significantly as a function of wound healing time, which corresponds to a stiffening of healing tissue compared to healthy tissue. The indicator $Δ$t and S (from MyotonPro__) are significantly different when HA was injected compared to healthy tissue, which also corresponds to less stiff tissue. Additionally, both IBAM and Cutometer__ detect significant biomechanical variations in superficial soft tissue related to tissue growth in all measurement regions. This first in vivo use of IBAM shows that IBAM could assess significant variations related to wound healing or regeneration mechanisms following HA injection. This study paves the way for the development of a simple, low-cost and objective device. Future clinical studies or other animal models should be carried out to confirm these results.

title: ROSE: A Shared Cross-Embodiment Facial-Motion Latent Space for Humanoid Robot Expression
abstract: Natural, coherent full-face dynamic expressions are central to making humanoid robots socially approachable, yet existing systems commonly realize only limited lip motion or scripted expressions. The limitation is both physical and algorithmic. A compact head leaves little room for densely packed, independently controllable actuation; meanwhile, learned systems often generate an avatar video, landmarks, or facial parameters and then infer actuator commands through visual retargeting. This render-and-invert path adds latency and artifacts, and it does not reliably transfer generated behavior to a physical robot. We present ROSE (RObot facial expression through Shared motion Embeddings), a framework that integrates biomimetic hardware, cross-embodiment motion representation learning, and multimodal motion generation. On the hardware side, we build a flexible tendon-sheath transmission structure that integrates 34 actuators into a 19.5 cm biomimetic head. By decoupling actuator placement from facial action points, it enables coordinated full-face expression within a compact volume. On the algorithmic side, ROSE-VAE learns an identity-independent shared facial-motion latent space from human, digital-human, and robot observations. ROSE-Flow directly maps text, audio, or their combination to trajectories in this motion space without using video as a generator input. ROSE-ACT then converts these trajectories into constrained actuator commands. Our system demonstrates how high-density biomimetic hardware and a shared executable facial-motion representation can jointly unify cross-embodiment learning, multimodal generation, and physical robot expression.

title: A Convergence Analysis of the Random Feature Method for Linear PDEs
abstract: The Random Feature Method (RFM) distinguishes itself among machine learning approaches to partial differential equations (PDEs) through its superior accuracy and computational efficiency. Nevertheless, the theoretical underpinnings of RFM remain incompletely elucidated. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of RFM within the framework of kernel methods, focusing on two principal aspects: (i) approximation by finitely many random features in Sobolev norms and the PDE residual seminorm, and (ii) estimation over the induced reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) from finitely many noiseless collocation observations. We relate both problems to kernel ridge regression (KRR) and establish upper and lower bounds in terms of the eigenvalues of the associated integral operators under the respective assumptions. Combining the approximation and estimation lower bounds, we establish a lower bound under simultaneous restrictions on the numbers of random features and collocation observations. We further quantify how activation regularity affects these eigenvalues, obtaining algebraic upper bounds for finitely smooth activations and stretched-exponential upper bounds for analytic activations.

title: Altermagnetism in moiré quasicrystals
abstract: Altermagnetism is a collinear compensated magnetic phase with zero net magnetization and momentum-dependent spin polarization. Quasicrystalline altermagnetism extends altermagnetism beyond periodic crystals, with noncrystallographic symmetries allowing high-order spin polarization patterns. Here, we propose a symmetry-based approach to realizing quasicrystalline altermagnetism by twisting collinear magnetic layers. Specifically, we demonstrate that the $30^{\circ}$-twisted honeycomb lattice bilayers form the dodecagonal quasicrystals supporting an $i$-wave altermagnetic phase. We further find that $45^{\circ}$-twisted bilayers preserving fourfold rotational symmetry support a mirror-driven $l$-wave phase with eight nodal lines. We characterize these altermagnetic patterns through plane-wave-projected spin-resolved spectral functions and spin-resolved conductances. Our work provides a systematic route to high-angular-order quasicrystalline altermagnetism through twist engineering.

title: Same Fix, Different Weights: Replicating Weight-Space Programming with Claude
abstract: Takehi et al. (2026) report that GPT-6 Astra, given the weights of small neural networks as text, can say what they were trained to do, repair them, and write new ones without training. I re-ran the core of that study with Claude Opus 5.5 in ten pre-registered experiments, with untrained-network and permutation controls and hand audits of every sandboxed code cell. Reading was mixed: Claude named 3 of 4 Atari games from policy weights and found the measured copying heads in 15/15 character-LM runs, but its answers about training data often followed priors. Unlike the original, it identified a sycophantic Gemma 3 270M finetune from weights alone in 6/6 runs. One-shot weight edits took a failing MountainCar policy from 0% to 100% success and a hovering LunarLander policy from 0% to 85.6%; zero-shot networks beat PPO at 100k steps on 4 of 5 environments, each implementing a textbook controller. With no training or forward passes, Claude wrote a 1.48M-parameter 9x9 Go network that won 85-94% of games against three PPO opponents. Given Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights and 10, 25 or 50 forward passes of 64 practice problems, Claude raised MATH-500 from 6.7% to 51.4%, 55.2% and 58.1% (+51.4 points at 50 passes, 95% CI [47.9, 55.0]; original 48.1%), GSM8K from 11.6% to 68.2% and IFEval from 22.2% to 54.2%. Unlike the original, which removed an internal loop direction, every edit acted at the output: it scaled the final norm, raising the effective sampling temperature, and lowered the logit of "Wait" while raising that of </think>. The norm scaling alone reaches only 20.9-22.1% on MATH-500. On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, no edit helped (-0.8 points), as in the original.

title: Layer-wise Linear Probing of an Encoder-free Audio-capable Language Model
abstract: Encoder-free audio-capable multimodal language models pro- vide a unique setting for studying how speech representations emerge inside a language-model decoder. In Gemma-4-12B, short waveform frames are projected directly into the shared embedding space, and all subsequent contextual processing is performed by the decoder layers. We use this architecture to examine where acoustic, phonetic, segmental, and paralinguis- tic information becomes linearly accessible across depth. Us- ing the TIMIT corpus, we extract all 49 representations from the frozen model, including the embedding output and the out- puts of its 48 decoder layers. We train linear probes for log- F0, log-energy, voicing, phone identity, word-onset structure, speaker identity, recorded speaker gender, and dialect-region labels. The results show a broad progression in linear acces- sibility. Acoustic properties are most strongly decodable in the early layers, paralinguistic attributes are most accessible in the early-to-middle layers, and phone identity and boundary- sensitive information reach their highest performance around layer 11. Several properties remain strongly decodable across broad near-peak regions rather than at a single uniquely optimal layer. In deeper layers, phone identity and closed-set speaker identity decline sharply, while voicing, log-F0, and gender re- main more accessible. These findings provide an initial map of how speech information develops when the decoder is the first contextual stage to process audio.

title: Jev-as-a-Reward: Validating Probabilistic Safety Judges for Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts. A confidence gate sends only uncertain verdicts to a stronger LLM judge, which leaves confidently passed harm in a blind spot. Policies can exploit this blind spot, and commercial judges release new versions. We propose a protocol that validates such a judge before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, and re-validates it after each judge change. We apply it to two versions of Jev, a commercial decision-only judge, and to an open guard classifier. Under the probability reward of Jev, passed harm shrinks in all 11 runs under the primary reference, mostly more slowly than caught harm, and concentrates in the blind spot. Binarizing this judge meets the escape criterion on Llama, and the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed under a second reference. Guard classifiers share this blind spot, and even frontier LLM judges catch at most one of 10 human-labeled confident misses. Without a trained reward model, the probability reward with a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033 at the final checkpoint.

title: From Vision to Interaction: Evaluating Dynamic Social Intelligence of VLM Agents in ALIVE-World
abstract: As AI agents are increasingly deployed in real-world applications and take on social roles, dynamic social intelligence, the ability to continuously perceive multimodal cues, infer latent cognitive states, intervene through embodied actions, and ultimately achieve social goals, has become essential. However, existing evaluations largely fragment social intelligence into text-based abstractions, static reasoning tasks, or embodied simulators that lack social dynamics. These approaches fail to capture the multimodal, continuous, and interpersonal complexity of authentic human interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce ALIVE-World, an embodied simulation environment supporting dynamic multimodal interactions encompassing egocentric vision, language, and non-verbal action. To provide socially grounded interactive feedback, we populate this environment with counterpart agents driven by a profile-conditioned, dual-system (intuitive-affective and logical-cognitive) architecture. Building upon this platform, we propose ALIVE-Bench to transform the assessment of social intelligence into a trackable quantitative framework. By deeply leveraging underlying environmental states and agents' internal variables, ALIVE-Bench systematically evaluates Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents across four critical dimensions: perception, understanding, influence, and outcome. Extensive evaluations reveal that dynamic social intelligence is fundamentally multi-dimensional and scenario-dependent. We identify a critical bottleneck between upstream perception and downstream social intervention, exposing VLM vulnerabilities in fine-grained proxemic awareness, adaptive intervention, and multi-party coordination. By uncovering these limitations and the diverse interaction strategies they produce, this benchmark provides actionable insights for the future behavioral alignment of multimodal agents.

title: Branch-and-Cut for Maximum $k$-Independent Sets with Spectral Bounds
abstract: We develop a branch-and-cut method for finding maximum distance-independent sets in graphs. Our approach solves a sequence of fixed-size clique problems, combining graph reductions with combinatorial and spectral bounds. We give a compact formulation, derive strengthened inequalities, establish conditions for using spectral information, and evaluate them in a comprehensive computational study.

title: Static Bounds on Thermal Fast Scrambling
abstract: Scrambling, the process by which initially localized quantum information spreads across an interacting many-body system, is a hallmark of quantum chaos and plays a central role in understanding black hole dynamics. In thermal systems, the chaos bound of Maldacena, Shenker and Stanford limits the exponential growth rate of out-of-time-order correlations to $2π/β$, assuming that time-ordered correlation functions factorize after a dissipation time. Establishing the corresponding rigorous logarithmic lower bounds on scrambling times at arbitrary fixed temperature has remained an open problem, most notably in disordered systems, where the Gibbs state depends on the same random couplings that drive the dynamics. Here we prove such bounds at every fixed temperature for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model and for random $k$-local spin systems, without assuming real-time factorization. Our approach uses the operator-size distribution of the square root of the Gibbs state to quantify how local probes modify its structure. This static information bounds the thermal correlator uniformly in time along the edges of its analytic strip in complex time, and analyticity then limits how rapidly scrambling can develop. For both families of models, we prove that with probability tending to one the scrambling time is at least $(1-ε)[β/(2π)]\log N$ for any $0<ε<1$, with the coefficient $β/(2π)$ suggested by the chaos bound. The bound holds for each fixed pair of distinct Majorana modes in the SYK model and for the target average of any fixed single-site source in the spin model. These results place the thermal fast-scrambling timescale on a rigorous footing and show how static properties of the Gibbs state can constrain real-time information spreading.

title: Detecting the pterygomaxillary disjunction using an instrumented hammer: A cadaveric study
abstract: Background: In many maxillofacial surgeries, the surgeon must perform a pterygomaxillary disjunction in order to separate the jaw from the skull. The disjunction is performed using an osteotome which is impacted with a hammer until its tip crosses through the pterygoid plates. To determine whether the disjunction has occurred and avoid complications, surgeons still rely on their proprioception. Methods: The aim of this study is to validate a vibroacoustic set-up constituted by an instrumented hammer equipped with a force sensor, aiming at detecting if the disjunction has occurred. To do so, fourteen osteotomies were performed in anatomical subject jaws. For each impact, the force signal was recorded and analyzed. A classification algorithm (Support Vector Machine method coupled with a cost matrix) was developed based on indicators extracted from the signal to determine whether the disjunction had occurred. Impacts were classified into two classes, one before and the other after the osteotome had crossed the pterygoid plates. To avoid undetected disjunctions a cost matrix was added to the algorithm. The coefficients from the matrix were chosen using by minimizing the Negative Likelihood Ratio. Findings: The algorithm was able to distinguish impacts before and after the disjunction with an accuracy of 96 %. Moreover, the instrumented hammer was able to detect the disjunction with a maximum delay of two impacts. Interpretation: These results pave the way for the development of a per-operative decision support system for the pterygomaxillary disjunction.

title: Triples in matroid circuits
abstract: We prove that, if $X$ is a four-element independent set in a vertically $5$-connected representable matroid $M$, then either there is a circuit of $M$ that contains at least three elements of $X$, or there is a representation $A$ of $M$ such that each column of $A$ has at most two non-zero elements and each of the columns indexed by $X$ has exactly one non-zero element. We also prove a version of this result without the connectivity assumptions.

title: Using an instrumented hammer to predict the lateral hinge fracture in high tibial osteotomy: A cadaveric study
abstract: Open-wedge High-Tibial Osteotomy is the most commonly employed technique addressing varus knee osteoarthritis. During this procedure, the osteotome passes through cortical and trabecular bone. A common complication is lateral hinge fractures, which depends upon when the surgeon stops impacting the osteotome. The aim of the present study is to determine whether an instrumented hammer can be employed to detect (i) the bone type (cortical or trabecular) surrounding the osteotome tip and (ii) when bone is fractured by the osteotome. Seventeen lower-limb specimens were obtained from nine fresh human anatomical subjects. The osteotome was impacted using the instrumented hammer until rupture. Each impact signal was recorded and analyzed. An algorithm was developed to detect the transitions between cortical and trabecular bone and vice versa. Detection was based on the relative variation of $τ$ derived from the force signal as a function of time as the time difference between the second___and___first impact peaks. The values of $τ$ were significantly lower in cortical bone compared to trabecular bone. Considering the arrival of the osteotome tip in trabecular bone during a medial, a difference of less than 2 impacts between the surgeon and the algorithm was obtained for 71% of the cases. For the lateral osteotomy it was obtained in 81% of the cases. This cadaveric study demonstrated that the instrumented hammer could prevent impacts leading to hinge rupture, which suggests that future clinical trials are warranted.

title: Discriminants and resultants of orthogonal polynomials
abstract: The concept of a linked pair of two sequences of polynomials, one of which is orthogonal, is introduced. Such a pair always has a resultant that factors. Two methods for producing such linked pairs are given: one for general orthogonal polynomials and the other for any polynomial in the Askey scheme. Generalized discriminants are introduced and evaluated, including a general product formula for each operator in the Askey scheme. A new notion of companion orthogonal polynomials is also introduced and used to evaluate the discriminants of orthogonal polynomials. These methods recover all known formulas for the generalized discriminants of classical polynomials and provide new ones.

title: Global bound-state spectrum and spin- and angular-momentum-dependent confinement in an inverse-$3/2$ magnetic quantum dot
abstract: We investigate the bound-state spectrum and confinement thresholds of a two-dimensional electron governed by the Schrödinger--Pauli equation in an inverse-$3/2$ radial magnetic-field profile. The radial problem reduces to the biconfluent Heun equation, but instead of restricting the solution to the quasi-exact polynomial sector, we impose the bound-state condition globally through a spectral Wronskian between the endpoint-selected Frobenius solution and the subdominant asymptotic solution. The resulting spectrum contains continuous nonpolynomial bound-state branches on which the known quasi-exact solutions appear as isolated exact points. In this global description, the polynomial index $N$ remains a termination index within the quasi-exact sector but does not uniquely label the spectral branches. An independent exact analysis of the continuum edge yields spin- and angular-momentum-dependent critical couplings that can lie below the quasi-exact restriction $U_0a>4$, where $U_0$ is the Coulomb-strength parameter and $a$ is the magnetic-profile length scale. These results establish quasi-exact solvability as a set of special analytic points embedded in a broader biconfluent-Heun spectrum with spin- and angular-momentum-dependent confinement thresholds.

title: A Soft Sponge-Pillar Electrode Platform for Motion-Tolerant Ambulatory EEG and Sleep Monitoring
abstract: Long-term wearable electrophysiological recording systems are essential for both clinical and real-world environments. While a wide range of wearable devices have been reported for electrocardiogram (ECG) and electromyogram (EMG) recording applications, most electroencephalography (EEG) measurements still require subjects to remain stationary while wearing rigid and uncomfortable equipment. Here, a soft and wearable sponge pillar EEG electrode is presented for long-term and motion-tolerant EEG recording. The electrode is composed of two layers of a carbon black (CB)-polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composite, where a firmer solid base assists in bypassing hair, enabling stable access to the scalp, while a porous sponge tip ensures comfort, reliable contact, and low skin-electrode impedance. Fabricated via a sugar templating process without microfabrication steps, the microporous sponge structure offers low modulus and significantly enhances the contact area with the skin when loaded with conductive gel. This allows the electrode to achieve a lower contact impedance of $1.62 \times 10^{4}\,Ω$ at 10 Hz, outperforming conventional gelled electrodes while maintaining gel stability for over 18 hours. With the electrodes integrated into wearable form factors such as headbands, headphones, and baseball caps, EEG signal recording during motion have been demonstrated, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 16.46 dB. These features establish the sponge pillar electrode as a promising platform for next generation wearable EEG systems, enabling comfortable, stable, and prolonged brain signal acquisition on ambulatory subjects and in naturalistic environments.

title: A General Theory of Nonparametric Response-Adaptive Randomization
abstract: Response-Adaptive Randomization (RAR) assigns incoming patients to treatments with probabilities that depend on previously observed responses. While most existing RAR procedures rely on finite-dimensional summaries of treatment performance (such as rates, means, or model parameters), we develop a nonparametric (NP) distribution-based framework in which the treatment outcome distributions are learned sequentially and adaptation is driven by their functionals. The framework naturally accommodates multiple treatments and is particularly suited to endpoints for which average effects may conceal relevant differences across the outcome distribution. We introduce an ethical NP-RAR rule driven by a pre-specified distributional score and a nonparametric extension of the multi-arm efficient randomized adaptive design (NP-ERADE) able to approach generic distribution-dependent targets selected according to ethical or inferential optimality criteria. We establish strong consistency and joint functional central limit theorems for the empirical treatment distributions, together with asymptotic normality of functional scores, estimated targets and allocation proportions. We further show that the NP-ERADE allocation proportions attain the semiparametric efficiency bound for the target. We develop post-trial inference for score contrasts and distributional features, including crossing locations, and investigate finite-sample properties, robustness and inferential performance via simulations.

title: Finite-order exponential mixing does not imply the central limit theorem for unique equilibrium states
abstract: Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold of dimension at least three, $φ:M\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and $R\ge2$ be an integer. We construct a $\mathcal C^\infty$ diffeomorphism $T:M\to M$ and an observable $f\in\mathcal C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ such that $(T,φ)$ has a unique equilibrium state $μ$ and $μ(f)=0$. The system $(T,μ)$ is exponentially mixing of order $R$ but not of order $R+1$ for Hölder observables, and $n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f\circ T^i$ does not satisfy the central limit theorem. The main results have been formalised in Lean 4.

title: The Interplay of Stellar Feedback and Gravity in the Wat01-S208 Star-forming Complex
abstract: To investigate the processes governing clustered star formation, we present a multi-wavelength study of the star-forming complex hosting clusters Waterloo 01 and [BDS2003]64 in Sh 2-208. Both clusters exhibit elongated morphologies, with radii of $\sim1.5$ and $\sim0.9$ pc, respectively, and are located at a common distance of $\sim3.5$ kpc. Wat01 displays hierarchical structure ($Q=0.6$) and signature of mass segregation ($Γ_{\rm MSR}=1.5\pm0.6$).
